LETTERS TO THE EDITOR 


I would like to compliment you on your Spring 
’84 editorial; you carefully displayed many of 
society’s specific flaws while giving us a wide 
range of examples. 

I agree with the philosopher who identified 
our “central problem” as our lack of being neigh¬ 
bourly- in the spiritual sense of the word - and 
charitable. More often than not, we tend to get 
too wrapped up in ourselves and fail to under¬ 
stand or reach out to our neighbours. Yes, we 
have come a long way, but we also have a very 
long way to go. Finally, I would like to commend 
you on your choice of cover photo. 

Dorothy Nielson 
Toronto, Ontario 

I appreciated your Spring editorial. I have been 
friends for a long time now with someone who 
possesses a disability. I have never really given 
it much thought but recently, I have begun to 
learn of the much deeper feelings that aren’t 
always evident. We often have pleasant and 
good times together but, on occasion, he feels 
moody and depressed and increasingly declines 
invitations to go out. 

He says that, at times, he doesn’t care what 
people think but, deep down, he is sensitive to 
society’s ignorance and society’s reaction to 
him. He would like to see this changed and be 
treated as “normally” as everyone else. 

My friend is a wonderful person but it is a 
shame and a sin when we, in society, treated 
disabled people as if they are freaks to be stared 
at and, in some instances, ridiculed. 

CONTENTS _ 

Summer 1984 


In actuality, your editorial makes me realize 
that it’s not really my friend who has the problem, 
is it? 

Harry Rokkos 
Etobicoke, Ontario

that preparing themselves, their staff, their 
parents, their campers and their physical site is 
really not that difficult. Most camp directors I 
know rise to a challenge. If one continually puts 
up barriers to integration, disabled children will 
continue to be isolated and not have the oppor¬

adulthood. Camp is an ideal setting fora child to 
be challenged and to grow and camp directors

Resources: 

1) In every province there is an agency working 
with physically disabled children and adults. 
Contact: Canadian Rehabilitation Council for 
the Disabled, 1 Yonge Street, Suite 2110, Toronto, 
Ontario M5E1E8 (416) 862-0340 to obtain name 
and address of the specific agency in your 
province. 

2) Contact: Canadian Association for the Men¬ 
tally Retarded,4700 Keele Street, Kinsmen Build¬ 
ing, Downsview, Ontario M3J 1P3 to obtain 
contact for local chapter or Association. 

3) Local public library may carry a selection of 
books relating specifically to “Special Popula¬ 
tions” or they should be able to order them for 
you. 


4) Colleges or Universities in your area offering 
related courses may have written resources. 
You may be able to use students in these 
courses in your program - perhaps for credit in 
their course. 

5) National Building Code - Supplement #5 - 
National Research Council of Canada, Ottawa, 
Ontario K1A 0R6. 

6) Provincial Building Code-Supplement deal¬ 
ing with accessibility for disabled persons - 
Contact the Provincial Ministry in charge of 
Building Codes. These codes will provide you 
with the proper dimensions and details when 
altering your physical site. 

7) Barrier Free Design Centre, c/o Muscular 
Dystrophy Association of Canada, 357 Bay 
Street, 10th Floor, Toronto, Ontario M5H 2T7 
(416) 364-9079. 

8) Canadian Red Cross - Water Safety Service 
Adapted Aquatics Program contact your local 
office.

EDITORIAL 

The Bible Tells Me son 

What does it mean to be Christian? What does it mean to be religious? What 
does it mean to be charitable or spiritual? What is truth? 

All too often today the guise of religion or Christianity is used to justify 
actions which may be hostile, uncharitable or inhumane. And the Bible is 
often cited as our authoritative source to legitimize many irrational attitudes, 
feelingsor behaviours.The disturbing reality is the frequency with which the 
Bible is quoted "out of context”; and the selectivity used in choosing those 
words or passages ONLY which tend to give credence or support to the 
human penchant of disparaging and denigrating others. Sadly too, certain 
Churches have often told its followers WHAT to think- using the Bible as a 
sourcebook - and not HOW to think critically in order to more sensitively 
confront the many moral decisions that will have to be made in one’s 
lifetime. Is the Bible truth? If it is, there are as many versions of truth as there 
are people who read it- not to mention that English versions use language 
which is sometimes in disagreement or contradiction (King James Version, 
The Revised Standard Version, The New English Bible and The New Inter¬ 
national Version). Imagine an original statement, made about 2,000 years 
ago, passed on from person to person or manuscript to manuscript, 
originally in Hebrew and later in Greek, and subjected to INTERPRETATION 
and TRANSLATION. At camp, groups often sit in a circle and play “rumour 
mill” where one person initiates a statement and whispers it to the next 
person who, in turn, whispers it to the next person and so on, until the last 
person repeats his or her version of the original statement; everyone laughs 
uproaringly when the initiator then states the original passage. This 
exercise is used as an important psycho-linguistic tool in helping kids 
understand human weaknesses and limitations in comprehending, inter¬ 
preting and professing truth AS WE PERCEIVE IT. While Christians and 
Jews believe the Bible to be the inspired word of God, God’s followers still 
must be required to think and use their own minds, consciences and wills. It 
is very often less secure to do so, but what an exciting and liberating 
experience in human responsibility! 

There is a trendy temptation today, perhaps due to a lack in education and 
moral reasoning, to attribute an infallibility to a particular mystic, leader, 
sage or guru. Many of these "leaders” preach absolute certainty on matters 
of truth (eg. some television evangelists, Falwell's Moral Majority, fundamen¬ 
talist Muslims, Jehovah’s Witnesses, Mormons, Rev. Sun Myung Moon, etc.) 
and require - no, demand, - that their followers obey their word absolutely, 
often by instilling fear, anxiety and guilt. Their insidious notion of truth or 
certainty leaves no room for faith; it demands, often through coercion, a total 
and blind acceptance and obedience. The use of fear to motivate people is 
no surprise, for it lies at the root of much human misery; fear is the 
underlying cause of war, fear is causing an escalation of nuclear arms, fear 
of the unknown keeps us from accepting those who are different. As the 
Bible aptly says, fear "has torment”; interestingly, one of Jesus’ most charac¬ 
teristic sayings is “fear not” and many times he grieved, asking “How is it 
that ye have no faith?” Jesus taught people not ONLY to worship Him but to 
follow God’s will, to share in and help actualize the Kingdom of God on 
earth. Unfortunately, many Churches find it easier to argue over Jesus' 
doctrines or divinity rather than do what He clearly said we must: love one 
another and establish justice among all the inhabitants of the earth. Jesus’ 
parable of judgement (Matt. 25) includes nothing about a person’s religious 
belief, sexual orientation or political ideology as criteria for God’s accept¬ 
ance or rejection on the last day. The question is: have you done God’s will 
by not closing your hand, even to the unlovable? “Not everyone that saith 
unto me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven, but he that doeth the 
will of my Father who is in heaven.” (Matt. 7:21) 

CONSIDER: 

■ In Iran, Khomeini’s men (mullahs) have executed approximately 30,000 
dissidents who refuse to conform to their beliefs; people who “refuse to 
interpret the Koran in the fashion approved by the mullahs .’’ (TIME, March, 
1984) 

■ In South Africa, where there are more orthodox believers in the dominant 
Protestant Church than in most countries of comparable size, people “who 
attend prayer and Bible meetings and take the Bible to be the inspired, 
inerrant word of God, the worst forms of racism and injustice reign supreme, 
fully supported by selected biblical texts.” (Tom Harpur) 

■ In Ireland, sectarian violence and hatred have not only pitted Catholics 
against Protestants for years but have instilled emotional instability, hatred 
and aggression as a fact of life for children growing up. The reconciliations 
that have occurred are too few and the message of good will is poorly 
communicated. 

■ In the United States, the “battle for racial integration and equality found its 


bitterest opposition in the ‘born-again’ Christians of the so-called Bible 
Belt” (Tom Harpur) 

■ The Middle East has seen Christians in conflict with Muslims, Muslim 
factions warring against each other, Palestinians and Jews against each 
other, and on and on. 

■ In Canada and the U.S., certain religions and sects refuse medical inter¬ 
vention and blood transfusions because of their interpretation of certain 
passages in the Bible; worse, however, is the imposition of this will on 
children who are too young to make informed, rational decisions - 
especially with respect to life and death! 

■ In India, violence between Sikhs and Hindus continues to escalate pre¬ 
dicated on religious factionalization, politics and territory; unfortunately, 
these homeland battles often occur on North American turf. 

How can the camping community help address the deep spiritual needs 
in every individual? As church attendance continues to decline (Gallup Poll 
in 1978 cited Catholic church attendance at 74% - today this figure stands at 
52% and is dropping) Professor Bibby of the University of Lethbridge says 
that “Canada can no longer be considered a Christian country in any 
meaningful way, since only about 40% claim any active Christian commit¬ 
ment - and a good portion of these are highly non-traditional in their 
beliefs." If our leaders cannot communicate faith to the young, the numbers 
of those who share faith will continue to decline. Camps can help through 
awakening in every child a keen sense of critical thinking - an ability to 
question logically and develop higher moral reasoning skills. In a language 
that is comprehensible, relevant to the twentieth century and stimulating, 
chapel talks and bible studies should help elevate a child’s understanding 
of our complex world - not simply instilling fears which legitimize OUR 
belief system! Children need to know that the measure of a spiritual or 
religious person lies in WHAT A PERSON DOES, not in how a person 
preaches. The hallmark of a spiritual person is one who treats others - 
whoever they may be and whatever colour, race, ethnicity, sexual orientation 

- with the respect and dignity every human being deserves. The parable of 
the Good Samaritan was very upsetting in Jesus’ time because people 
hated Samaritans and were taught to "have no dealings” (John 4:9) with 
them. The term had always had a strange and ironic resonance because of 
its inherent contradiction; “good Samaritan” is like the repulsive term “holy 
war”. Jesus defined goodness by the measurement of peoples’ deeds- not 
their words, so the parable of the priest and Levite who kept their robes 
clean and their images respectable by walking on the far side of the road to 
avoid the man who had fallen among thieves is important in that the man 
was helped by the lowly Samaritan. Too many people in the Christian 
community are more concerned with respectable appearances than acting 
with compassion, charity and responsibility. The Bible, as a historical test, is 

- in and of itself - neither good nor bad. The Bible (or Koran, Gita, Tao, 
Hibraic Holy Books etc.) is a vehicle which, if used inappropriately can 
actually justify hate, war, homophobia, rape, incest and child abuse. The 
Bible however, can be used to promote rational, critical thinking in children’s 
minds to facilitate more responsible and compassionate growth to adult¬ 
hood; the many stories, miracles and parables CAN and often DO promote 
moral learning, moral reasoning and higher moral thinking. Many people 
have selectively quoted and interpreted 2,000 year-old biblical passages to 
justify their discomfort with homosexuality; the irony is that many of these 
same people eat shellfish, wear red, eat pork, apply lipstick and refuse to 
cover their heads in Church. You see, it all depends on how the Bible is 
used. One way of helping children learn kindness is by doing kind deeds. 
Help children learn understanding by doing something for others; don’t 
instill fear and create anxiety and guilt by arbitrarily reciting only selected 
passages. The Bible CAN be used to help fill a spiritual void, a meaningless¬ 
ness in life, if only, as leaders, we apply the central themes to our camp 
programmes and measure worth and charity by our behaviour. Condemna¬ 
tion of others is too common, too easily justified and, unfortunately, is a 
boomerang. "At whatever point you judge the other, you are condeming 
yourself” (Rom. 2:1). Of course, loving acceptance is a boomerang also; 
whatever we do to our neighbour, for good or evil, we do to ourselves. Jesus 
feels the human pain of those whose needs we have rejected, people who 
have been put down: “I tell you this: anything you did not do for one of these, 
however humble, you did not do for me.” (Matt. 25:45). Measure a person by 
actions, not words; the measure of worth is in how a person lives not in what 
a person says or how a person preaches. To this end, the Bible can be a 
resource which promotes love, faith and understanding and can alleviate 
human suffering and misery; our energy, through camp programming and 
spirituality should reflect these ideals and values.

la cause! 



CAMPING ADVISOR 


Over the course of two summers working as a 
camp counsellor, I have found that I sleep much 
more soundly at camp compared to the city. 
Some friends of mine have experienced the 
same thing; is there a known reason for this? 

S.B., Halifax, Nova Scotia 

There are probably several reasons for this 
phenomenon; current theory relating to our 
body’s bio-rhythms holds that it may well be a 
“negative ion effect”. Negative ions are freely 
abundant in our natural environment: beside 
lakes, on campsites and especially near water¬ 
falls. Our natural bio-rhythms seem to ebb and 
flow best within negative ion environments; 
cities with concrete, steel and flourescent lights 
abounding have an abundance of positive ions. 
Some experts say this accounts for our dis¬ 
rupted sleep patterns in the city and our “sound” 
sleeps at camp. Many people in the city actually 
purchase negative ionizers for precisely sleep 
reasons. 

Secondly, we expend tremendous physical 
energy at camp - much more so than in the city. 
It’s quite obvious and natural, then, that our 
bodies NEED more recuperation time at camp 
and therefore, because we are tired from so 
much activity, we sleep easier and more soundly 
at camp. 

Thirdly, when we alter our diet and our regular 
routine we necessarily alter our biological func¬ 
tions which include sleep. Diet has been shown 
to have a profound effect on sleep patterns. 

★ ★ ★ 


What is the most watched spectator sport in 
North America? 

J.B., Edmonton, Alberta 

Baseball! The 37th annual attendance figures 
have just become available and baseball has 
surpassed horse-racing as the number 1 spec¬ 
tator sport in North America; horse-racing has 
been first in annual attendance of major events 
for the last 31 years! In 1983, baseball attracted 
over 78 million spectators compared with 75 
million for horse-racing. What about hockey, 
you ask? Hockey was at the very bottom with 
only 20 million fans in 1983 - even greyhound 
racing was more popular! 


In discussing rainy-day programming with 
camp staff, we wondered: can one catch a cold 
from the rain? 

A.V., Harrow, Ontario 

There’s actually a medical institute in Great 
Britain solely examining and attempting to 
isolate causal factors of the “common cold". 
Their answer: no, one cannot catch a cold from 
being wet! They have actually had experimental 
subjects walk at length, without clothes, in the 
rain with no effects at all associated with colds. 
Actually, we’ve heard that some camps practice 
this same procedure! 


At a recent conference, you stated that Dr. 
William Masters said that “homosexuality is a 
natural expression”. How can it be natural when 
it seems obvious that males and females “fit” 
together with procreation as our motive and the 
result of the male-female union? 

M.L. Willowdale, Ontario 

In the first place, many homosexuals can and 
often DO exercise their procreative feelings and 
conceive (female) or impregnate (male); further¬ 
more, many heterosexuals either choose not to 
procreate or cannot bear offspring and this fact 
shouldn’t undermine their sexuality, sexual 
orientation or sense of maleness and female¬ 
ness. People shouldn’t be made to feel guilty 
over choosing NOT to have children; very few 
professionals in medicine, psychology or psy¬ 
chiatry would call procreation an “instinct", (as a 
matter of fact, scientific studies show that 
“mothering" is not even an instinct but “parent¬ 
ing" is, meaning that males and females can 
learn to elicit responses we generally associate 
with “mothering"). Also, given the fact that many 
people say that “procreative sex is natural", why 
is it that 99.9% of sexual activity in North 
America is RECREATIVE, not PROCREATIVE? 
As leaders, we have to speak more openly on 
responsibility and contraception, hoping that 
people will enjoy their sexual expressions with¬ 
out the added burden of V.D. or unwanted preg¬ 
nancy; in 1982 in Toronto, there were 8,033 live 
births ... and 8,166 abortions! Somehow we're 
not doing our job as leaders and educators in 
preaching the ethics of respect and respon¬ 
sibility! 

With respect to what is natural, I would say 
that what is natural is what feels “right and com¬ 
fortable ” for you at any given time - provided it is 
predicated on honesty and consent and does 
not violate the criminal code. You see, to a gay 
person, same-sex attraction is both normal AND 
natural; to a heterosexual, for example, such an 
attraction is foreign and therefore “unnatural”. A 
gay person would see our opposite-sex attrac¬ 
tions as different, foreign and therefore “unnat¬ 
ural” to him or her. I guess we're fortunate to be 
in the majority and enjoy and take for granted 
the media representation - television, books, 
movies, magazines, romance stories, socializa¬ 
tion - which concentrates and focuses on 
heterosexual relationships with all the inherent 
joys and hardships. There’s nothing really wrong 
with that except that we tend to oppress and put 
down those whose attractions are different from 
ours and this is unfortunate, disrespectful and 
unacceptable! The same was true, years ago, of 
society never portraying black-white relation¬ 
ships in any meaningful way; the situation is 
rapidly changing but there certainly is still a 
need for more genuine representation; we must 
learn to keep in mind that “different" does not 
mean “wrong"or “bad”; it simply means “not the 
same" 

Years ago, people believed in a philosophy 
called the Doctrine of Signatures (some actually 
still do) which dictated that “shape determines 


function". As silly as it may sound, people 
believed that cauliflower was good for the brain 
because it resembled a brain; we obviously 
know a great deal more today! And people like¬ 
wise believed that because a penis and vagina 
“fit", it is therefore a “natural function" If, for 
argument’s sake, it was suggested that the 
shape of a penis also fits in a hand, or a jar, or a 
mouth ... at what point does “natural" become 
“unnatural”? This was the essence of Dr. William 
Master’s thesis; it’s important to remember that 
what is natural is what is natural FOR EACH 
INDIVIDUAL, providing no one is being hurt, the 
law is not violated and the behaviour is con¬ 
sensual!

we will endeavour to publish the most interest¬ 
ing and provocative ones. Address all letters to:

Camping, 1806 Avenue Road, Suite 2, Toronto, 
Ontario M5M 3Z1.

Glen Bernard Camp 




The Report to the 30 th General Council on 

Human Sexuality 

Summarized by James Taylor 


In August, the 30th General Council of The 
United Church of Canada will receive a report 
on human sexuality. While the report itself will 
not be distributed before formally presented to 
the General Council for consideration, this un¬ 
official summary has been prepared for mem¬ 
bers of the United Church so that they may be 
informed about the Report. 

It needs to be understood that this report is 
part of a continuing discussion. It is not a final 
statement, nor a retouching of previous docu¬ 
ments. It is a new document seeking to assist 
church members in the continual struggle to 
discover what it means to be a follower of Christ 
in today’s world - a world in which sexuality 
pervades all aspects of life, while understanding 
of sexual roles and responsibilities keeps 
changing. 

An Overview of the Report 
In essence, three themes run through the 
report 

1. Sexual drives and feelings affect everyone. 
They are not an optional extra which can be 
arbitrarily separated from Christian life. 

2. It is what we do about those drives and 
feelings that matters. There is a recurring em¬ 
phasis on the need to make responsible deci¬ 
sions. 

3. The model for those decisions comes from 
Christian faith- based on scriptural understand¬ 
ing and our relationship with God. 

Those themes are explored in five chapters. 
To facilitate study and discussion, each chapter 
works with four elements: 

□ as objective as possible a description of the 
present situation; 

□ a selection of real-life stories illustrating the 
dilemmas; 

□ an exploration of insights from relevant scrip¬ 
ture passages; 

□ affirmations, offered as general guidelines or 
markers for behaviour. 

The summaries that follow cover only some of 
these elements in each chapter. 

Sexuality and Selfhood 
This chapter defines why the United Church 
should be studying sexuality at all. 

Sexuality pervades everything in present life. 
Like the colour of one's eyes, it is an integral part 
of being human. We cannot choose whether or 
not to have sexual feelings - the choice is what 
we will do with the feelings we have. 

Yet attitudes towards sexuality vary widely. 
How we think and talk about maleness or 
femaleness affects our behaviour and relation¬ 
ships, and the kind of persons and society we 
become. 

Similarly, ways of expressing sexuality vary. 
The traditional expression has been in marriage. 
However, sexuality within marriage is not avail¬ 
able to all. Some choose not to be married; some 
have marriages end in divorce or death; every¬ 


one is single for part of life, at least in the 
adolescent years. What happens to sexuality in 
those situations? 

Biblically, sexuality can be seen as a gift from 
God. 

But the Bible also recognizes that sexuality 
can be a dilemma, a gift contaminated by sin. Yet 
though no one is immune to its potentially des¬ 
tructive forces, God’s grace can transform the 
dilemma into a promise, a relationship which 
reflects the convenant relationship we have 
with God. 

Marriage 

Within the church today, two attitudes toward 
marriage seem to predominate. On the one 
hand, faced by increasing statistics of marriage 
breakdown and divorce, some people call for 
firm directions. Others suffering in oppressive 
marriages, hurt by divorce or the death of a 
spouse, or who can no longer accept traditional 
roles, call for more compassion, understanding 
and flexibility. 

In that setting, the church can make an impor¬ 
tant contribution, in a renewed understanding of 
the meaning of Covenant. 

That concept of Covenant is founded on our 
relationship with God. It involves the total 
person; it is not always voluntarily chosen; it 
demands unconditional faithfulness; it is de¬ 
pendable. We can never fully earn nor deserve 
the relationship; in return, it must never become 
self-serving, but must turn us outwards to 
others. 

While there can be many kinds of relation¬ 
ships between persons, in marriage these 
aspects of the closeness of a Covenant relation¬ 
ship with God are worked out in daily life. 
Intimacy 

Perhaps of all the chapters, this one is most 
likely to be misunderstood. For intimacy here 
does not mean sexual intercourse. Rather, in¬ 
timacy is the sense of closeness that one can 
have with another person. Like sexuality, it is a 
universal desire. Unfortunately, also like sexual¬ 
ity, it may be abused or distorted. 

Intimacy is more than sex or marriage, though 
intimacy may be a goal of both of those. The 
birth of a child, the death of a loved one, can also 
be incredibly intimate moments when barriers 
come down between people. Similarly, there is 
intimacy in counselling and in friendship. 

Surprisingly, to some, the Bible encourages 
intimacy. God is revealed as one who is deter¬ 
mined to have an intimate relationship with a 
chosen people. Jesus with his disciples, Mary 
with God, David and Johnathan, Ruth and 
Naomi - all offer models of intimacy for Chris¬ 
tians. 

The search for intimacy, therefore, is also # a 
spiritual journey. It is dangerous, because it 
holds a potential for being hurt and for hurting 
others, and perhaps for needing to change. In it 


is also the potential for increasing maturity. 

The chapter suggests that the Christian 
Church has not dealt well with intimacy. Fearing 
the dangers, it has largely ignored the values 
that can accompany intimacy. For example, the 
last General Council, in 1982, expressed con¬ 
cern about “situations of emotional intimacy 
leading to potential genital expression.” Taken 
literally, that would exclude the natural and 
growing intimacy that should develop during 
courting before marriage. 

How should the church respond to a single 
adult’s need for that sense of intimacy which is 
the opposite of alienation? How should an 
adolescent struggling towards self-identity learn 
about intimacy? What about a 50 year old who 
loses the intimacy of 25 years of happy marriage 
when a spouse dies? In none of these instances 
does intimacy necessarily mean sexual inter¬ 
course. Yet these very real needs have often 
been overlooked. 

Sexism 

If sexuality can be positive and creative, 
sexism is the other side of the coin. This chapter 
describes sexism as a destructive force in 
which the ideals of a Covenant relationship are 
distorted into inequality and exploitation. 

The chapter stresses particularly ways in 
which sexism becomes so integrated into social 
structures that it often goes unnoticed as it 
undermines people’s behaviour. 

As with other matters related to sexuality, 
sexism results in varied reactions within the 
church. 

Some are apathetic. They don’t understand 
why others are upset, nor do they see what it has 
to do with them. 

Some are anxious. They recognize that some¬ 
thing is happening, and they fear that changes 
are coming which will affect them. 

Some are antagonistic. They see the kinds of 
changes that are being demanded. Consciously 
or unconsciously, they also see these changes 
as a threat to their present power, influence, or 
position. They resist. 

Some are active. Having seen sexism as a 
subtle and insidious force affecting all of their 
lives, over which they have no control, a force 
which contributes to pornography, prostitution, 
rape, wife battering, sex in advertising, and 
media exploitation of women, they devote their 
energies to denouncing and combatting sexism. 

While the church has, in recent years, become 
more aware of sexist attitudes, it is not free of 
them. From the congregational level to the 
national offices, women continue to be under¬ 
represented in decision-making roles. 

Sexual Orientation 

Because of the traditional disapproval towards 
homosexuality, few heterosexual people even 
realize that they may know homosexual men 
and women personally. 


6 



The reaction to homosexuality, as to sexism, 
is often fear and anger. Christians may charitably 
avoid expelling homosexual persons from their 
congregations, but they continue to treat them 
as persons needing either repentence or cure. 

Homosexual persons resent accusations of 
promiscuity and child molesting, pointing out 
that these offences are far more often committed 
by heterosexuals. 

This chapter neither censures nor promotes 
homosexuality. It calls for more open discussion, 
more study of the origins and nature of homo¬ 
sexuality, and particularly more study of the 
Scriptures together, with the aims of increasing 
mutual understanding, and dispelling some 
fears. It sees the result of such study not as a 
loosening of sexual standards, but as a deepen¬ 
ing. 

An appendix examines those scripture pas¬ 
sages commonly identified with homosexuality. 
The chapter itself deliberately chooses for study 
a passage from Acts 10 that does not deal with 
homosexuality as such, but rather as a means of 
discerning basic principles about the ways in 
which the church has learned to deal with per¬ 
sons excluded from Christian fellowship. 

Affirmations Recommended 

In approving the Report for presentation to 
General Council, the Division of Mission in 
Canada endorsed a series of affirmations as the 
basis for “general guidelines for use in the 
United Church of Canada.” 

These included, on “Sexuality and Selfhood": 

• that “sexuality is a gift from God ... a primary 
way of relating to ourselves and to one another 
... the way that God has chosen to continue the 
human race.” 

• that “the giving and receiving of affection... is 
a basic human need.” 

• that “even in the midst of ambiguity, we are 
called upon to make responsible decisions” 

On “Marriage”: 

• that in marriage, “Christians make a covenant 
with one another and with God” and that "in 


Christian marriage a man and woman give them¬ 
selves to each other in the full intention of a 
lifelong commitment." 

• that “sexual intercourse in marriage is in¬ 
tended to be... exclusive.” 

• but also that “there are many couples in 
committed relationships other than marriage to 
whom the church is called to minister in love.” 

On “Intimacy”: 

• that “all people experience a hunger for inti¬ 
macy" and that "it is in our experience of the 
intimate God that we find the grace and possi¬ 
bility of intimacy with one another." 

• in intimate relationships, “the importance ... 
of respecting the integrity of others, of setting 
limits on our actions.” 

• that singleness and/or celibacy may be “a 
state in which people may find intimacy and 
fulfilment." 

On “Sexism”: 

• that “the intention of God for all persons is full 
equality in both our personal and social lives." 

• that “God calls us as a church to eliminate all 
forms of sexism... in the life and worship of the 
congregations, presbyteries, conferences and 
national structures of The United Church of 
Canada." 

• that the “structuring of society can be re¬ 
deemed and eventually transformed through the 
grace of God and the struggles of those willing 
to face... sexism.” 

On “Sexual Orientation”: 

• that “all believers in Christ are accepted as 
full members of the Christian church regardless 
of their sexual orientation.” 

• that the church is “called to initiate and 
encourage communication and discussion with 
homosexual believers about sexuality in order 
thatfellowship may be increased and misunder¬ 
standing, fears and hostilities lessened." 

This report has been published under the au¬ 
thority of General Council Executive. Reprinted 
with permission of the office of the General 
Council of The United Church of Canada.

par: Colette Pouliot-Marier,

dente de I’Association, Mme Jocelyn Palm, que

directrice du Camp Claret, au poste de presi¬ 
dente du comite des camps depression 
frangaise. 

Qu’il me soit permis de rappeler que ce 
comite qui a 6te mis sur pied a I’automne 1974 a 
pour but d’assurer une presence active des 
camps francophones et de faire entendre le 
point de vue des camps de langue frangaise au 
sein de (’Association. 

Certes, depuis les dix dernieres annees des 
efforts ont 6te accomplis afin de repondre aux 
besoins des camps frangais et aussi pour 
rejoindre les membres francophones. Parrrii les 
actions mises de I’avant, rappelons, entre autres,

cation entre les camps le langue frangaise au

anglaise au niveau national. C’est dans cette

Focus on Pre-Camp: The Camper! 

by: Catherine Ross, Camp Mi-A-Kon-Da 



Camp Mi-A-Kon-Da 


Pre-Camp ’83 was progressing much the same 
as any other pre-camp week. The entire staff 
was busily occupied making the most of the few 
days before the campers’ arrival. Linda, the 
programme director, was finalizing lists, menus 
and destinations for the staff overnight excur¬ 
sion to review their canoeing and camping 
skills. The nurse was compiling her list of 
campers currently on medication. In the kitchen, 
‘Cookie’ was checking deliveries and experi¬ 
menting with new recipes. The tripper was 
selecting his tripping canoes and checking his 
equipment. Former staff were careful to include 
new counsellors in their conversations while 
the new counsellors were seeking answers to 
the dozens of questions about traditions and 
procedures. Each evening the section heads 
met briefly to review the day’s progress and plan 
the next day’s programme. Nothing must be 
overlooked. We must find time for the waterfront 
search pattern, a fire drill, an evening pro¬ 
gramme planning session, writing up progress 
books, familiarizing counsellors with their new 
campers and preparing welcome signs to greet 
each tent group. 

A Letter for Pause and Reflection 

Amidst this hive of activity a letter arrived. 
Hurrying to the dining room in response to the 
five minute warning bell, I tore it open and 
glanced at the contents. The words brought me 
to a halt on the path and I began to reread it more 
carefully. The letter was from a lifetime friend, 
Linda, whose eight year old daughter was due to 
arrive at our front dock in a few days for her first 
residential camping experience. I had watched 
Jennifer, the youngest of three and only daugh¬ 
ter, grow from infancy to girlhood - her parents’ 
pride and joy. Linda had decided to share with 
me her thoughts and concerns as she prepared 
to send Jennifer to camp and away from the 
security and protection of their loving home for 
the very first time. 

On reading the letter, my first reaction was 
one of humility and apprehension. ‘How dare I 
presume to accept such an awesome respon¬ 
sibility?’ But I quickly remembered that I was not 
carrying this burden alone. It is one that I share 
with a caring and competent staff. As my confi¬ 
dence and ego resurfaced I thought - we are 
accepting a grave responsibility presuming to 
care for the physical, emotional and spiritual 
well-being of each camper, but what a privilege 
to influence and shape the lives of these eager 
young people. In a final effort on the last night of 
pre-camp to put all our preparations into per¬ 
spective, I shared Linda’s letter with my staff. Let 
me share the letter with you. 

'You and I go back a lot of years. We have been 
campers and counsellors together and shared 
the burden on a portage. I feel now I can share 
some of my ‘first year mother’ anxieties with you. 

I know it will be helpful for me if you know them, 
and perhaps might be helpful for you in antici¬ 


pating and understanding some of the thoughts 
that I m sure are not unique only to this mother. 

There is still time to prepare Jennifer well 
physically. Her clothes will be plentiful, clean 
and well labelled. Her flashlight will have new 
batteries - the best, so as not to burn out.Her 
notepaper will include stamped, addressed 
envelopes home! Knowing I have time to do this 
with her before she leaves pleases me and 
makes me feel useful. 

There is not enough time left forme to prepare 
her well emotionally. Then again - maybe she is 
- maybe I’m not! I wonder about such motherly 
things as: who will understand when she has 
trouble sleeping at night that an extra hug and 
kiss will soon bring pleasant dreams? Who will 
understand how to deal with her shattered 
world if she receives a rebuff from her peers or 
idolized counsellor? Who will give her the much 
needed and cherished praise fora job well done 
or new challenge met? Who will be able to deter¬ 
mine if a hurt is really physical or a cry for 
emotional uplifting? For the next two weeks, 
who will nourish and mother her if I am not 


there? These next two weeks will change and 
mould her as no other two weeks in her life! I 
truly believe the who will be you and your hand¬ 
picked staff. 

Her brothers keep telling me Jennifer is lucky 
to be going to camp. We think of you and wish 
you well each summer - that goes double this 
year! 

P.S. Jennifer’s never written a letter. Please help! 

Each camper is a special person to his 
parents and family. In his time at camp it is our 
responsibility to continue the nurturing and 
development of these beloved children. We can 
do this by attending to each child individually, 
listening to him and sharing with him at some 
point ineach day, whether he demands it or not, 
some of our time. By doing so we show him that 
we care and we reinforce his positive self 
image. Let us commit ourselves to do our very 
best for all the Jennifers and Johnnys now 
packing their suitcases, excited and a little 
apprehensive, as they dream of their first holiday 
at camp. 


8 




OPERATION 

RALEIGH 

CANADA 

For young men and women across Canada, 
between the ages of 17 and 23, there is an 
exciting venture taking place throughout the 
next four years, involving adventure, travel and 
an opportunity to do something for others! 

Operation Raleigh is a 15-phase operation 
(three to four months each), spanning a total 
period of four years, and made possible through 
the co-operation of more than 30 countries. In 
all, over 4,500 young people will take part, and of 
this number 100 will be chosen from Canada. 

The program which involves exciting scienti¬ 
fic, conservation and community programs on 
land and sea, will provide many opportunities for 
the young to overcome problems, seek new 
challenges, and develop their talents. In short, 
they will be encouraged to discover leadership. 

Each phase of the trip will include 200 ven¬ 
turers representing participants from all of the 
countries involved. It begins in November 1984, 
when the specially equipped Flagship sets sail 
from Merseyside, bound for North Carolina. 
Upon arrival in the United States, Operation 
Raleigh will take part in the celebrations of the 
founding of English speaking America 400 years 
ago. Accompanied by vessels and sailing ships 
from participating nations, the flagship will then 
sail to the Caribbean, Central and South Amer¬ 
ica, Antarctica, Australia, New Zealand, Oceania, 
Asia and Africa on its voyage of scientific dis¬ 
covery and human achievement. 

The majority of all expenses for Canadian 
participants will be funded directly by the Oper¬ 
ation Raleigh Foundation, but each participant 
will be asked to raise through local sponsors, 
and supporters, 1 /3 of the cost which amounts 
to about $2,000.00. (Total cost $6,000.00) 

Under the patronage, and very keen interest 
of H.R.H., the Prince of Wales (Prince Charles), 
Operation Raleigh is seeking young people who 
have determination, energy, common sense, 
adaptibility, maturity and physical endurance. 
The selection procedures culminate in an eval¬ 
uation weekend at one of three locations in 
Canada. These will be held each year to select, 
and prepare the participants for one of the 15 
phases over the next four years. 

John Latimer of CCA has been invited to 
become a member of the Board of Directors of 
Operation Raleigh Canada, and is therefore 
anxious to inform readers of CANADIAN CAMP¬ 



ING of this exciting venture. If more information 
is desired, as well as applications, write: Opera¬ 
tion Raleigh Canada, The Weston Centre, 22 St. 
Clair Avenue East, Toronto M4T 2S3. 


NATIONAL 


Nicholas Joseph 


LIFEGUARD 

SERVICE 

CERTIFICATION 

by: Kelly Lendsay, NLS Chairman 

NLS is the lifeguard training course of the 
Royal Life Saving Society Canada. Other awards 
of the Society, such as the Bronze Medallion 
and Bronze Cross, are designed to educate in 
life saving. The distinction between life saving 
and lifeguarding is important. 

The aim of the Royal Life is to make “Every 
Swimmer a Life Saver”. With water rescue and 
resuscitation skills, life savers can provide im¬ 
mediate assistance to someone in trouble. Life 
saving skills are all applicable to an informal 
situation where the activity is recreational and 
may be unstructured such as that at a cottage. 
Out of the broadly based group of life savers, 
come those who aspire to be lifeguards. 

The RLSSC defines a lifeguard as a person 
who is responsible for a given area and/or 
aquatic activity. Potential lifeguards must have 
life saving skills and knowledge. The RLSSC 
Bronze Cross and minimum 16 years are the 
prerequisites to the National Lifeguard Service 
course. The NLS Course is offered in three 
options: pool, waterfront or surf. 

Camps will discover that staff with this certifi¬ 
cation are invaluable in the encouragement of 
appropriate behaviour in the aquatic environ¬ 
ment. NLS lifeguards can also provide further 


in-service training to those on your staff who 
hold life saving awards and have yet to acquire 
the extra skills and knowledge of a certified 
lifeguard. 

NLS courses are offered through RLSSC 
programs across Canada. Summer camps who 
wish to offer the NLS program to staff and 16 
year old campers have two choices. The camp 
has on staff an NLS Instructor who teaches the 
40 hour course in blocks of time when partici¬ 
pants are available. This is ideal as camp 
recreational swims and camp facilities offer 
endless opportunities for practical experience. 
The second choice, would be to import an NLS 
Instructor who would offer the course prior to 
the arrival of campers, as a part of pre-camp 
training. Perhaps a third choice is to encourage 
the staff to take the pool option at their local pool. 
While some of the material will be specifically 
oriented to lifeguarding and supervision in a 
pool, most of the material is appropriate to all 
applications. The camp waterfront director 
should review the specific material that applies 
to your particular camp waterfront once the staff 
are at the camp. 

The NLS course includes: lifeguarding skills 
and techniques, maintenance of the pool or 
beach (depending upon the option chosen), 
public relations, search procedures, aquatic 
emergency care, program administration, legal 
aspects and government regulations. 

Information concerning the availability of NLS 
courses may be obtained from your provincial 
Branch of the RLSSC. 


9 


CROUP DYNAMICS EXERCISE 
Responding to those "Difficult" questions 

By: John Roberts 


Handbooks for Camp Counsellors provide a 
wide variety of answers on countless numbers 
of questions asked by campers, or posed as a 
result of behavioural differences. But there are 
very few books on the Camp Director’s shelf 
which provide answers for Counsellors when 
asked questions of a personal or value judge¬ 
ment nature. How do Counsellors cope with 
very sensitive questions about sex, drugs, 
morals, religions? 

In pre-camp, Directors and staff spend con¬ 
siderable time discussing swimming, archery, 
fire emergencies, campfire programs, canoe trip 
safety, the stars, bedtime procedures, discipline 
problems and story-telling. But in many camps, 
very little time is given to helping the Counsellor 
learn ‘how to handle’ questions which, although 
very important to campers, are better left ‘un¬ 
touched’. There are some publishers who feel 
that reference to sexual or moral attitudes are 
too personal, or judgemental, and should there¬ 
fore not be discussed for fear of losing sales. 

But time should be spent in pre-camp ... and 
Counsellors should be encouraged to express 
their feelings and values as to how to respond to 
very natural questions from growing and easily- 
influenced young people. 

Camp leaders might consider this exercise 
for use prior to camp, or at specially called 
meetings during the summer with Counsellors 
and Leaders-in-Training. 

1. Initially indicate to the group that the purpose 
of this exercise is to give the staff an oppor¬ 
tunity to verbalize their views as to how 
certain personal questions and problems can 
best be handled within their own group of 
campers. At the same time, the staff will be 
encouraged to express their own personal 
views on each of the topics, after the 'experts’ 
have provided what they feel to be the ‘model’ 
answer. 


2. The staff and/or L.I.T. group is divided into 
sub-groups of three or four. 

3. Each sub-group is given a four-question 
topic (see some examples below). Allow 15- 
20 minutes for each group to arrive at a 
consensus answer for each of the four parts 
of the question. The question is repeated 
(along with the conditions), and a spokes¬ 
person from the sub-groups gives the ‘model’ 
answer. 

4. After the response has been given for each 
topic, the audience is then encouraged to 
question the respondants (the “experts”) as 
to the appropriateness of their answers. 

5. Should the Camp Director have philosophical 
differences with the answers, these should 
also be expressed at the time, or in summary 
following the discussion on each topic. 

The following are some suggested TOPICS 

and examples. If used, they should be pre¬ 
written on the four cards to be given to each 
sub-group. 

The TOPIC (or question) should be written at 
the top of each of the four cards. The balance of 
material on each card varies according to age of 
the camper, and attitudes or practices of the 
Counsellor. 

Topic - Capital Punishment. 

Is Capital Punishment right? 

Card 1 - From a 9 year old to a Counsellor who 
strongly believes in Capital Punishment. 

Card 2 - From a 9 year old to a Counsellor who 
is firmly opposed to Capital Punishment. 

Card 3- From a 15 year old to a Counsellor who 
strongly believes in Capital Punishment. 

Card 4 - From a 15 year old to a Counsellor who 
is firmly opposed to Capital Punishment. 

Topic - God. 

Is there a God? 


Card 1 - From a 9 year old to a Counsellor who 
firmly believes in the existence of God. 

Card 2 - From a 9 year old to a Counsellor who 
has some serious doubts about the existence of 
God. 

Card 3- From a 15yearold to a Counsellor who 
firmly believes in the existence of God. 

Card 4 - From a 15 year old to a Counsellor who 
firmly denies the existence of God. 

Topic - Virginity. 

Are you a Virgin? 

Card 1 - From a 9 year old to a Counsellor who 
is a virgin, but wonders to himself if he’s 
“normal”. 

Card 2 - From a 9 year old to a Counsellor who 
is not a virgin, and whose sexual encounters 
have only been for physical enjoyment, with no 
love or feeling involved. 

Card 3- From a 15 year old to a Counsellor who 
has not had sexual intercourse and does not 
believe in it before marriage. 

Card 4- From a 15 year old to a Counsellor who 
has engaged in sexual intercourse with his girl¬ 
friend who he loves. 

Topic - Masturbation. 

Is Masturbation wrong? 

Card 1 - From a 12 year old to a Counsellor who 
masturbates occasionally and feels very guilty. 
Card 2 - From a 12 year old to a Counsellor who 
is not uncomfortable with the fact that he 
masturbates. 

Card 3- From a 15 or 16 year old camper or L.I.T. 
to a Counsellor who feels masturbation is sinful 
and wrong. 

Card 4- From a 15 or 16 year old camper or L.I.T. 
to a Counsellor who has no feelings of guilt, and 
is comfortable with his own sexuality in mastur¬ 
bating. 

Topic - Abortion. 



10 



CANADIAN CAMPING ASSOCIATION 
ASSOCIATION DES CAMPS DU CANADA 



ANNUAL REPORT 
1983 

RAPPORT ANNUEL 


PRESIDENTS REPORT 

Lots of camping activity during the past year and this is reflected in 
the projects, conferences, programs and workshops of the Provin¬ 
cial Associations. Congratulations to each Provincial President and 
the Boards and Committees who carry out the various activities. 
Taken altogether, we have to be ethusiastic about the Canadian 
perspective in camping. 

The CCA Board and Committees have also had a busy year. I 
urge you to read these reports and I know you will be pleased to 
learn more concerning: 

■ Plans for CC A’s 50th Anniversary in 1986 from Cliff Labbett, Past 
President of CCA 

■ Special projects for 1985 International Year of Youth from Hugh 
Phillips of Edmonton 

■ CCA Involvement in the 1987 International Congress in Washing¬ 
ton from our representative, Janet Adamson, Toronto 

■ Ongoing work of the Education Committee, chaired by Dorothy 
Walter, Toronto 

■ The strides in Publicity and Promotion led by Chairman, Marnie 
Ellis of Montreal 

■ Successes of the Publications Committee under the able leader¬ 
ship of Wendy Wren and Judy Richards, Toronto 

■ The response to “Canadian Camping” is evidence of the work of 
the indefatigable Jay Haddad, Toronto 

■ Barry Lowes, Chairman of the Immigration Task Force who 
developed and has maintained excellent working relationships 
with the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission 

■ Bruno Morawetz of Peterborough, chairs the Archives Commit¬ 
tee and watches over our past history which is maintained at 
Trent University 

■ Leadership Development projects have been held in several 
provinces and you’ll get specifics from Paul Potter, Chairman 

■ The Environment Committee is functioning with Jean Funk of 
Edmonton at the helm 

■ Standards Chairman Brian Law of Winnipeg will advise of his 
work over the past year. 

And, of course our three hard working Vice Presidents, George 
Matthews (East), Ken Willis (Central) and Terry Burkhalter (West) 
have each communicated to their respective Provincial Associations 
and are acknowledged. Ken replaced Louis Jean who resigned after 
accepting a position with ACQ. Thank you George Ross, Treasurer 
for your work, advice and contributions. One of the unsung heroes 
of CCA is Jan James, CCA Secretary. While most of Jan’s work is 
evidenced in the Minutes, she also makes valuable contributions to 
many areas of CCA operations. 

We are grateful to the Camping Association of Nova Scotia for 
hosting and sharing in this 1984 Annual Meeting and Conference. 
This opportunity to meet with others has also been enjoyed during 
1983-84 in British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario and Newfoundland; 
thank you all for your warm welcomes to CCA delegations. 

Fitness Canada have provided invaluable funding opportunities 
and we are appreciative of this support. We recognize that our 
unique organization would be limited significantly without these 
contributions. Thank you Shirl Willette and your Ministry. 

Marjorie Booth, our Executive Director has the challenge to 
weave all CCA volunteers and their projects into a workable whole. 
Thank you for your cheerfulness Marj in the face of the demands 
made of you. 

Thanks to each of you who work to make camping in Canada 
more widely known and available to Canadians. 


EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR S REPORT 

The applause from the International Camping Congress had almost 
died down when 1983-84 began last April. Nevertheless, the 
Canadian Camping Association/Association des camps du Canada 
had already geared up for our next major effort, National Camping 
Day on April 14th. 

Marnie Ellis and her capable team of provincial volunteers carried 
out their respective tasks to begin the difficult job of achieving public 
awareness of Camp Counsellors and organized camping. Following 
this first effort, Marnie determined the plans for the next National 
Camping Day - March 21st, 1984. The Board were informed in 
October and the provincial PR volunteers were asked to follow the 
promotion plan used and developed for April 1983. 

Publications continue to be a significant effort of the Association. 
The loyal volunteers, Wendy Wren and Judy Richards continue the 
task of maintaining an accurate inventory of books as well as mailing 
out the orders across the country. The highlight of this year was our 
newest publication the Counsellor-in-Training Manual. This publica¬ 
tion was produced in two versions, an instructor’s manual for CIT 
Directors and a “Workbook” version for the CIT’s themselves. Sales 
have been extremely good since we required a second printing by 
June 30th! The volunteers who contributed this manuscript deserve 
our congratulations. 

Terry Burkhalter, our Western Vice President, did an effective job 
as Executive Workshop Task Force Chairman. This CCA/ACC 
Workshop, held at Bolton Camp in October, was our first in-depth 
executive training for provincial presidents and vice presidents since 
1976. The major recommendation from this event is to continue this 
type of training in the future. 

Three opportunities for my professional development were 
provided by the Association in 1983/84. In May, I was able to spend a 
week at the American Camping Association Headquarters in 
Bradford Woods, Indiana. The week provided new insight into 
potential development areas for a national camping association. I 
was indeed fortunate to spend time with virtually all the ACA 
executive staff. 

In early June, I completed the 2nd year of the Canadian Institute 
of Organization Management at the University of Western Ontario. 
The theme of this course was “Management Dynamics” and dealt 
with effective motivational techniques for volunteers. 

The Association also allowed me to attend the American 
Camping Association National Convention in San Diego in February. 
These experiences all serve to expand my knowledge and under¬ 
standing of environment within the Association. 

The part-time staff of the Association has undergone some 
change during this year. Mary Roy left the CC A/ACC in September 
after eight years of loyal service. Our typist, Sharon Freedman, also 
resigned during the fall prior to the birth of her second child. Thank 
you both for your hard work and continuing interest in the camping 
movement. 

We were fortunate to recruit Irene Knapp as our new Secretary/ 
Bookkeeper in October. Irene has settled into this rather unique role 
very well - adapting to the various demands with great enthusiasm. 
Thank you Irene for your tremendous support and interest. 

Next year could be called “Great Expectations”! With Interna¬ 
tional Youth Year beginning in 1985, we have plans for three special 
events: a Youth Camp Director Institute in January, a special IYY 
edition of Canadian Camping in Spring and a special celebratory day 
program at all CCA/ACC Member Camps in August. 

The CCA/ACC will hold another Promotions Workshop for 
provincial delegates in October to finalize our publicity plans for 
1984-85. 


Jocelyn Palm 


Fitness Canada continues to provide more than financial assis¬ 
tance. The consultant for much of 1983/84, Mr. Shirl Willette, has 
supported our efforts enthusiastically throughout the year. 

The CCA/ACC is more than meetings, minutes and mailings - it 
is MEMBERS. As I participated in events across Canada this year I 
am grateful for the interest, excitement and commitment of the 
leaders of the camping movement. We have much to be proud of 
due in no small part to the outstanding efforts of our national 
volunteer Executive, Board and Chairmen. Thank you for your 
dedication - it is my pleasure to work with all of you. 

Marjorie Booth 


NEWFOUNDLAND & LABRADOR 

During our 1983 AGM it was announced by Newfoundland’s 
Minister of Culture, Recreation and Youth that the NLCA was to be 
granted office space at the Provincial Recreation Centre, Torbay. It 
is there that most other youth, recreation and sport association 
offices are housed. Hopefully this will provide us more opportunities 
to promote our association as well as a home for our operations and 
resources. 

We have experienced a substantial turnover in our Bord of 
Directors this year with the addition of six new members. This 
includes Judy May of Comer Brook, our west coast director which 
is a position that we have had difficulty in filling over the past several 
years. Over the past year many of us have had to make adjustments 
in order to become acquainted with the NLCA. To this end our 
Executive have been reviewing terms of reference and constitution 
items in order to involve more people in our activities. Our focus will 
be to strengthen committees and to make our association a truly 
provincial one. 

Through the diligent efforts of Barb Taylor we have produced an 
up-to-date directory which is available through our provincial office. 

Our secretary, Levi Hehaney and his wife attended the American 
Camping Association Conference in San Diego in February. They 
were very enthusiastic about the activities and sessions which they 
attended, and, as usual were disappointed that there was not 
enough time to attend more sessions. Such conferences help to 
charge up our commitment to the camping movement and serve to 
remind us of the great impact we can have on youth. Levi was also 
instrumental in arranging for Grant Kerr, President of OCA, to 
attend our meeting of March 29 where he provided us with some 
information on the operations in other provinces. We found his talk 
quite interesting as he touched on many of the issues which NLCA is 
facing. It is interesting to observe that many of our associations have 
similar problems. 

Myself and Janice Stroud, a new board member, attended the 
CCA Executive Development Workshop at Bolton Camp, Ontario, 
in October. We both found the course very beneficial and it allowed 
us to become more familiar with scope and range of CCA. 

We are now preparing for our Annual Meeting and Spring Work¬ 
shop which will be attended by Marjorie Booth and Dorothy Walter. 
Following our AGM we will be offering our counsellor leadership 
course on the last weekend of May at Rotary Sunshine Camp. 

A proposal has also been forwarded to Employment and Immigra¬ 
tion Canada for funding of a summer project which would supple¬ 
ment our visitation and provincial visibility efforts. We hope to reach 
more camps with this project in an effort to have a clearer picture of 
camping in Newfoundland & Labrador. 

Wallace Gregory 


NOVA SCOTIA 

The Association received an intern under the Summer Canada 
Employment Program during the summer of 1983. Being accepted 
into this program automatically makes us eligible for a staff person 
for the summer of 1984 and 1985. 

By having this person on staff, we were able to develop two 
training programs for camp counsellors; one at Camp Hilles on the 
Mainland and one at Camp Aite Breagh on Cape Breton Island. Both 
were well attended and very successful. 

In addition, several training programs for individual camps were 
carried out by the intern for Association Members. 

In cooperation with Canoe Nova Scotia, the Association put 
together and published a new book entitled “Canoe Routes for Nova 
Scotia”. This was placed on sale in the summer of 1983 and we look 
forward to this book increasing our income over the next few years. 

One of the results of having a staff person working with the 
Association was the increase in book sales for our Association and 
for the Canadian Camping Association. Books were available at all 
Association events and at individual camps when the camps were 
visited. We will carry out the same format in the summer of 1984. 

In December we were pleased to have the President of CCA with 
us for our bi-annual meeting and dinner. Jocelyn carried greetings 
from CCA and was the main speaker of the evening. 

All in all it was a successful year with planning already underway 
for the CCA Board meeting in May/84. A major event will be staged 
at the Nova Scotia Agricultural College from May 4th to the 6th. 

George Matthews 


NEW BRUNSWICK 

The year 1983 has been both a productive but trying year for those 
involved with the New Brunswick Camping Association. As presi¬ 
dent it is certainly a pleasure to report that the Board of Directors 
provided the membership with the largest calendar of events ever 
offered and in doing so were able to maintain a stable financial 
position without the support of traditional government grants from 
the Department of Youth and Recreation. 

Highlights of the year included: 

• five development workshops for camp staff and outdoor educa¬ 
tors including - Counsellor/Director Weekend, Canoe Instructor 
School, Winter Outdoor Skills Institute, Fall Weekend, and 
Camp Committee Workshop. We are indebted to CCA for 
providing funding for Consultant/Advisors for two of these 
events. 

• the recognition of three individuals, two camps and one agency 
through our newly created awards program designed to honour 
the volunteers who have made significant contributions to 
camping in New Brunswick. 

• a new format and improved quality of our quarterly bulletin 
“Camping News”. 

• the launching of a membership campaign. 

• the granting of a charitable tax number that has allowed for a 
major fund-raising program to begin. 

The above noted highlights combined with the routine duties of 
our six ongoing committees provided for a stable base and positive 
year for those involved with NBCA. 

One of the most difficult tasks the Board of Directors had to 
contend with was the association’s financial position. The sudden 
loss of government grants from the Department of Youth and 
Recreation due to provincial budqet restraint left the association in 



a fragile financial position, however, through careful planning and 
corporate support the association ended the year with a small 
operating surplus. 

Other minor problems occurred throughout the year, however, 
the positive happenings certainly out numbered the setbacks and 
the year can certainly be termed a success. 

Thanks are extended to the many individuals who have contri¬ 
buted to the continued growth of NBCA. Your efforts are not 
unnoticed as without this volunteer commitment our association 
would not be the healthy, progressive organization it currently is. 

Ian R. Fowler

ONTARIO 

Throughout 1983, we celebrated the 50th Anniversary of the 
Ontario Camping Association. It was a year marked with a number 
of excellent Association events including a creative 50th Anniversary 
Party/Annual Meeting in the Spring; a very successful Counsellor 
Conference (1000 registrants); an involved summer of camp visita¬ 
tions (some 70 camps visited); the production of a great new OCA 
History - to be available to all. It was a year-long celebration. 

The OCA with its 200 camp members, 300 individual members 
and some 50 commercial members continues to provide quality 
camping experiences for children, youth and adults. The Board and 
Executive have worked well and several administrative changes 
were introduced. A major task currently underway is the purchase 
of computer equipment for our Office. And the Committees, and 
Task Forces of the Association offered a variety of workshops and 
seminars - all of which were well attended. 

A new film was commissioned and will be used for educatiorV 
promotion throughout the Province. Our Legislation Task Force 
continues to monitor changes in Government policy that will affect 
camps. And new attempts in regional development have been 
implemented to increase the awareness and visibility of the OCA 
across the entire Province. 


MANITOBA 

The year of 1983 is gone but has provided an even stronger base for 
the Manitoba Camping Association. We are particularly pleased by 
the improved participation of members - individuals, camps and 
organizations. As the value and need of the MCA becomes more 
known, we anticipate further participation. 

There are several events that merit specific comment. I will try to 
do these chronologically. 

First of all, it was terrific in January, 1983, to have 20 Manitobans 
travel to the CCA International Congress in Toronto. Manitobans 
gained a lot and gave a lot to this event. Special mention goes to 
Brian Law, who chairs the National Standards Committee. 

In early May, the MCA had the pleasure of hosting the CCA 
Board. In conjunction with their visit, Marg Law put together a 
terrific conference that saw 100 camping folks involved. The quality 
of the sessions was high as was the enthusiasm of the participants. A 
special treat was, Don Starkell relating his super canoe trip from 
Winnipeg to South America. He well illustrated the saying, “Life is an 
adventure or nothing at all”. 

The MCA Sunshine Fund had another fantastic year. The 
Winnipeg Free Press ran weekly articles on camping and kids. The 
people of Manitoba were generous in their support of the Sunshine 
Fund. Over $50,000 was raised with about 300 kids helped in going to 
camp. Kathy Taylor, as chairperson of the Sunshine Fund, did an 
excellent job. Bettie Heindl admirably handled the operation of the 
fund. Together, the MCA had a team that made *83 the best year in 
all aspects for the Sunshine Fund. Look out *84! 

The summer, as always was a busy time for camps. Modest 
increases were reported across the province. Visitations were made 
by the MCA for Standards Association. Terry Burkhalter was in 
charge of this with strong support from Bettie Heindl and the 
volunteer visitors. Terry is also the Western Vice-President of the 
CCA. 

September saw the MCA Board meet for a day to project plans 
and programs for the coming year. It was a helpful time as each 
member had an opportunity to express their concerns and dreams 
for the association. At the end of the day, there was a spirit of 
optimism for the MCA and its mandate. 

In closing, I would like to express gratitude to the many people 
who have made the MCA a strong voice for camping in Manitoba. 
One way this voice is heard is through our excellent newsletter, the 
Manitoba Camping Scene, edited by Cliff Derksen. Thank you to 
Bettie Heindl, who gives us strong support in the office. And, finally 
thank you to Marc Bruyere and the Manitoba government for their 
support of the MCA. We look to *84 for another strong year of 
camps and camping in Manitoba. The MCA wilt be a significant 
factor in making that happen. 

Bryan Hill 


SASKATCHEWAN 

For Saskatchewan our attentions have been focused on two aspects 
of work. First is the completion of our “Directory of Camps” for the 
province. Secondly we have been working on an exemption from 
the “minimum wage” legislation in the province. 


For the Directory of Camps, many hours have been put into the 
compiling of names and research to find camps in the province. In 
some cases camps are of very small duration and seemed to be 
hesitant of what the association could do for them. The SCA 
launched this project to the public as a co-ordinated effort with 
National Camping Day, March 21st. The Directory seems to be well 
received, having many requests to fill. 

Our second and most ambitious project was the application to the 
Provincial Government for an exemption under the Labour Stand¬ 
ards Act from “minimum wage” guidelines and hours of work. A big 
thanks goes to Marj Booth who prepared the brief, National office 
for the hours of research and to the other provinces who offered 
their support and assistance in compiling information. We are very 
appreciative of this solidarity shown by camping people across the 
country. I think a message is clear as to the strength and quality of 
camping in Canada. For Saskatchewan at least this means survival 
to the camps. Hopefully the camps not in the association at present 
will realize the value of their provincial association and the national 
federation. 

Other events for the year also included a conference on standards 
and accreditation of camps. Our entire system was revamped and 
updated, a job that will have positive effects for camping in 
Saskatchewan. The sessions held March 31st, in Saskatoon were 
very productive. Most of the camps that are presently accredited are 
due for renewal this summer. 

Saskatchewan, however, is still struggling along. We are trying to 
grow and share with our members a better camping scene, better 
resources, better leadership and a sense of pride in being a 
“Camping person”. 

David Godwin 


ALBERTA 

The Board of Directors held five meetings between the 1983 and 
1984 conference dates. The executive also gathered at other times 
for special tasks. 

A completely revised constitution was drafted and ratified by your 
Board for presentation and voting at this year’s AGM. Exemption 
from the Labour Legislation Act for camp counsellors on minimum 
wage and overtime pay was achieved. This will hopefully be 
maintained on a yearly basis with the Department of Labour. 

Programs and Leadership - Three regional workshops were 
held in addition to the annual conference. Over one hundred and 
twenty (120) participants and twenty-three (23) volunteer leaders 
contributed to the great success of these events. 

Four newsletters were published on a new format. The high 
quality of the newsletter has been well received by the membership. 

Committee Projects and Area Reps - In addition to the 
Education and Communication Committees, Standards, Member¬ 
ship, Conference, Research and Development were all active in their 
respective areas. A tremendous amount of volunteer time and effort 
has gone into these various committees enabling the Association to 
function smoothly and accomplish the myriad of tasks necessary for 
our advancement. 

The Area Reps who have the difficult task of keeping in touch with 
all the camps at the local level and who are the “representatives at 
large” for the Association continued to keep a follow-up on member 
camps in their areas, assist with camp visitations and sit on other 
standing committees. 


Thank-You’s - On behalf of the Board of Directors, I would like 
to thank the Outdoor Recreation Section of the Provincial Recrea¬ 
tion and Parks Department for their continued financial and moral 
support. A special thanks as well to Marjorie Booth, Executive 
Director of the Canadian Camping Association for her continued 
support and liaison with our Provincial Association. 

I would also like to thank the Board of Directors for their 
dedication and support over the past year. It is the strength of this 
fine group of volunteers that makes our Association the fine one it is. 

Michael Kenny 


BRITISH COLUMBIA 

The highlight of our activities inB.C. was our annual conference held 
at Camp Squamish March 16-18. The CCA Executive were able to 
schedule a meeting here to coincide with the conference, so we were 
able to draw on their skills and experience for a number of 
workshops. Our special guest was Jay Haddad, who did not only a 
really effective workshop entitled “Sexual Values and Attitudes in 
Camping”, but also brought his audio-visual presentation “The 
Universal Child”. It was a delight to have Jay with us for the weekend 
and a chance for many of us to tell him directly our appreciation of 
his efforts as editor of “Canadian Camping”. 

The consensus of opinion, I think was that this was the best 
conference we have had in some time and we are starting now to 
plan for next year. 

In other areas, a considerable amount of work has been done this 
year to re-evaluate our camp standards document and streamline 
procedures. This was much needed and a revised version should be 
ready for this summer. 

The other important developing in B.C. this year has been the 
creation of a regional section of BCCA on Vancouver Island. We 
have long felt the need for regional sections in this province and now 
the first concrete steps in this direction have been taken. 

David Adair
