50th ANNIVERSARY TASK FORCE 

1983 has been a busy year commencing with the highly successful 
International Congress jointly sponsored by CCA and OCA for this 
first ever function. Having been President of CCA when this 
concept was first established and working through its very difficult 
birth, it was very satisfying to see it come to fruition under a very 
capable and hard working committee. 

I have been given the responsibility of the initial planning of 
suitable activities to mark CCA’s 50th anniversary in 1986. Since 
contact has been made with many of the CCA Past Presidents and 
current provincial executives for ideas their response has been 
good. Since definite plans are not yet formulated the following ideas 
will be the basis of our anniversary celebrations: 

1. Kite flying across Canada. 

2. Be a part of the annual July 1st celebrations in Ottawa. 

3. Tie in with National Camping Day and sponsorship be private 
industry in a salute to Children’s Camping across Canada. 

4. Official recognition from UNESCO for camping’s contribution 
to protection of our environment. 

5. Across Canada campfires. 

Clifford Labbett 


ARCHIVES COMMITTEE 

The most important action has been the “brown bag” approach to 
the collection of Archival materials. Each Provincial Association was 
sent a large brown envelope marked “Archives” under which are 
listed the kinds of materials that should be saved and placed in the 
envelope for mailing at a later date when the envelope is about to 
burst. 

It seems essential that each President encourage his Archives 
Chairman to be alert to the necessity of collecting materials which 
would be of interest to later generations or to students doing 
research on camping for his province. 

Archivist Bemadine Dodge, Trent University, Peterborough, 
Ontario, K9J 7B8, will always be happy to receive materials of this 
kind, and it is hoped that each Association will diligently collect 
Archival material from its own members. 

Bruno Morawetz, Ph.D. 


EDUCATION COMMITTEE 

This report reflects action and progress made toward having the 
“Curriculum for Camp Directors” a viable resource. The curriculum 
is seen as an incentive for those who wish to pursue knowledge at a 
self-directed pace. The committee is addressing that issue. 

The content of the curriculum, having been confirmed by the 
provincial representatives last year, meant that the committee 
needed to turn its attention to resources, guidelines and methods for 
assessing individual progress toward the goal of professionalism. 

The document has now been put on word processing and we are 
investigating the “packaging” of it. In a survey to provincial 
associations, we now have an indication of what topics can be 
implemented provincially and what becomes a national responsi¬ 
bility. This is seen as assisting the planning of learning events on both 


levels. Since September, the focus of committee work has been to 
develop a bibliography; write guidelines for the use of the curriculum 
and in accompanying form to assist individuals to document their 
progress in covering the topics. Compiling of supportive resources 
has become a task for the committee. 

Our research indicated that video taping was too costly a venture 
therefore we are encouraging the Education Committee in each 
province to tape sessions at conferences and workshops to help 
increase major resources. We will be developing guidelines. 

“Director Education” is a challenging assignment and action plan 
for the near future is to (a) support the development of learning at a 
national level and (b) to encourage provincial initiative. 

I continue to praise the members of this committee who work with 
diligence and insight. Our progress is significant. My sincere 
appreciation is extended publicly to Stan Talesnick, John Wilkinson, 
Marjorie Booth and Jan James our Board liaison person. 

Dorothy Walter, Chairman 


ENVIRONMENT COMMITTEE 

October 1983 saw a fresh start for the Environment Committee. The 
following projects have been initiated: 

• revised Action Plan for the committee 

• submission of news items for the CCA/ACC Newsletter, or for 
provincial newsletters 

• review of current Environment Canada information 

• recommendation that the CCA develop an ongoing liaison with 
the National Trail Association 

• initiated correspondence with several forestry industries to 
determine what materials are available for CCA camps to use 

• reviewed the proposed Energy Camp; recommended that the 
CCA pursue a joint venture with the Terry Fox Centre in 
Ottawa 

• drafted the “CCA Environmental Ethic” 

I am looking forward to the development of environmental 
guidelines for campsite management, and the acceptance of the 
“CCA Environmental Ethic” in 1984. 

A special thanks go to Jan James, Executive Liaison, and to 
Marjorie Booth, Executive Director for their ongoing support. 

Jean Funk 


EXECUTIVE WORKSHOP 
TASK FORCE 

As reported in the 1982/83 CCA/ACC Annual Report our Task 
Force scheduled a Volunteer Executive Development Workshop at 
Bolton Camp and Conference Centre near Toronto, October 13-15, 
1983. The workshop addressed the following problem areas: 

• short term planning 

• decision-making (concerns, etc.) with volunteer boards 

• organizational development 

• problemsolving 

Arnold Cohen, Winnipeg, was the workshop leader/facilitator for 
our group. Our group consisted of two people from each province 
where possible along with the CCA/ACC elected executive. 



After summarizing the results of a questionnaire sent to partici¬ 
pants ahead of time, the following issues of leadership and manag¬ 
erial styles were highlighted: 

• decision-making 

• problemsolving 

• conflict resolution 

• communication 

• teamwork skills 

• planning 

As a tool, Cohen used the book, The New Managerial Grid (by 
Robert R. Blake and Jane S. Mouton, Gulf Publishing, 1978) to lead 
us through an intense experiential process. 

The intent of the workshop was to increase the participant’s skills 
in Effective Management Techniques . The premise for this workshop 
was that if we could improve the managerial abilities of association 
leaders, they would be more effective in their various leadership 
roles at the provincial national levels. 

Results of the workshop were tested immediately by participants 
who were involved in the 24-hour CCA/ACC Board of Directors 
meeting. During this meeting, the communication and planning 
activities of several members had changed significantly from 
previous meetings. 

Officially this task force has completed its responsibility according 
to the CCA/ACC ACTION PLAN. In the evaluation questionnaire, 
several persons encouraged a continuation of an executive develop¬ 
ment workshop every two years for the purpose of getting to know 
each other better, (particularly in lieu of changing representatives 
and personnel on the Board of Directors) and to constructively look 
at the issues of leadership and managerial styles as listed above. 

As the outgoing chairman of this Task Force, I will be recommend¬ 
ing to the Board of Directors an ongoing plan to continue working 
toward benefits that were an integral part of our October 1983 
experience. 

Terry Burkhalter 


FRENCH LANGUAGE COMMITTEE 

During the past year, the Editor of Canadian Camping continued the 
practice of producing the Editorial in both official languages. 
Additional efforts were made to include other articles in French and 
English. 

The Public Relations and Promotion Committee also improved 
the National Camping Day information for use in francophone 
communities in Canada. 

Pauline Rondeau resigned as Chairman at the end of this year due 
to severe time restraints. We look forward to welcoming the new 
Chairman of the French Language Committee, Colette Pouliot- 
Marier to the next Board Meeting. Colette plans to continue with the 
tasks of generating articles in French for Canadian Camping and 
establishing priorities and procedures for translation. 


Ken Willis

IMMIGRATION TASK FORCE 

The protocol worked out between the Federal Ministry of Employ¬ 
ment and Immigration and the writer, together with the Executive 
Director, during our meeting in Ottawa, has continued to serve well 
the needs of Canadian camps wishing to employ some foreign camp 
counsellors. Year by year these procedures are becoming used and 
accepted by camps across Canada, making the hiring of foreign 
camp counsellors a smooth operation. We appreciate the continuing 
support and co-operation we have received from the federal officials. 
Whenever a problem has arisen, they have been quick to help. 

Few problems occurred during 1983, when they did arise they 
were due to camps not following the protocol step by step. 

We have given three undertakings to the Federal Ministry: 

1. That camps will endeavour to follow faithfully the steps as set out 
in the protocol. 

2. That every effort will be made to hire a “Canadian” before request¬ 
ing permission to employ a foreign camp counsellor. 

3. That camps will provide basic statistical information to their pro¬ 
vincial associations, which will be collated by the Canadian Camp¬ 
ing Association office and forwarded to this Ministry. 

This statistical information is confidential and imperative if we are 
to continue to justify our requests. 

We urge you to provide the statistical information requested. 
The statistics compiled by the Federal Government are in the 
chart above. 


Barry Lowes 


1987 INTERNATIONAL CAMPING 
CONGRESS 

The Second International Camping Congress, is planned for March 
3-5,1987, in Washington, D.C. The Canadian Camping Association 
is jointly sponsoring this event with the American Camping Associa¬ 
tion. To this end, I have been representing the CCA at the Steering 
Committee meetings and Program Committee meetings. 

The Theme has been established - “Our Fragile World - A 
Challenge for the Outdoor Community” Plans are proceeding very 
well and the following organizations have indicated that they will be 
Joint or Cooperating Sponsors: 

I the American Camping Association 
the Canadian Camping Association 
the Jamaica Camping and Hiking Association 
the National Camping Association of Japan 
the Alliance for Environmental Education 
American Association of Health, Physical 
Education, Recreation, and Dance 
the American Nature Study Society 
the Association of Experiential Education 
the Council of Outdoor Educators of Ontario 
Christian Camping International, U.S. Division 
Cooperating the European YMCA Camping Group 

the National Recreation and Park Association 
the National Society for Internships and 
Experiential Education 
the World Alliance of YMCAs 
the World Association of Girl Guides and 
Girl Scouts 

The purpose of this Congress is stated as follows: 

“The Second International Camping Congress is an event to bring 
together the practitioners of the outdoor experience movement 
from many nations and related organizations to examine the 
elements of our fragile world which challenge the organized 
camping, environmental, and experiential education community to 
impact participants for future action ” 

Further publicity and news of this event will be appearing in future 
editions of Canadian Camping magazine. 

Janet Adamson 


INTERNATIONAL YOUTH YEAR 
TASK FORCE 

The IYY Task Force was struck in March of 1983. Five committee 
members from across Canada met for our initial meeting in Toronto 
on April 16-17, 1983. During this initial meeting 3 tasks were 
completed; namely, to define our purposes, discuss theme and logo 
of IYY and develop possible projects which committee members 
could coordinate in helping CCA celebrate IYY in 1985. 

A second IYY Task Force meeting was held on October 22-23 to 
delineate and commit ourselves to projects developed during the 
initial meeting. Three nation-wide projects were defined in some 
detail. These projects include: 

1. National Celebration Event: a special summer day in Aug. of 1985 
where all campers in CCA help celebrate the international year of 
youth. Program kits for the themes of fitness, environment, his¬ 
torical roots and peace will be developed by the IYY Task Force. 


2. Youth Camp Director Institute: proposed for Jan. 31-Feb. 1,1985 
at Bolton Camp, Ontario, this Institute will help youth camp 
directors to develop managerial and leadership skills and to learn 
how to deliver the curriculum for the professional development 
of camp directors. 

3. Special CCA Magazine Edition: an entire issue of Canadian 
Camping will be devoted to our youth. Themes of this issue will 
include peace, fitness, environment and historical roots. 

Our next meeting, April 18-19,1984, will be devoted to coordinating 
and implementation of these 3 IYY projects for CCA. 

Hugh Phillips

NEWSLETTER COMMITTEE 

Canadian Camping completed Volume 35 with quarterly issues for 
Spring, Summer, Autumn and Winter. The feature articles covered 
a broad range of topics and the readers continue to respond through 
Letters To The Editor. 

Members from across the country have contributed articles and 
photographs. We are now in the enviable position of having too 
much material for some issues. 

The newsletter featured a special theme issue for Winter ’84 on 
the environment. This kind of focus will result in recruiting new 
writers who have particular expertise to share. 

The task of producing CANADIAN CAMPING is very much a 
team effort. Special thanks to Marc C6t£ who contributes to the 
layout and photo needs of the newsletter. In addition, Therese Wong, 


our typesetter, takes a special interest in helping us produce an 
attractive finished product. Finally, Ken Smith at the National Sport 
& Recreation Centre guides the newsletter through the printing and 
mailing process in Ottawa before it reaches the members. 

Next year we look forward to your contributions so that Canadian 
Camping will reflect our members from coast-to*coast. 

Jay Haddad 


PUBLICATIONS COMMITTEE 

The CCA Book Store has enjoyed a fantastic year. Gross sales have 
increased by $8,776.00 over the previous year. This is evidence of the 
need for this service and also the support being received from CCA 
members. 

The CIT Manual and the CIT Instructor’s Manual written by 
several CCA members and donated to the Association has 
increased the volume of sales significantly. Legacy to A Camper and 
the Woodsmanship Leaders 9 Guide , both donated by the authors, 
continue to boost profits. This underscores the need to develop 
books which can be published by CCA. 

We acknowledge the assistance of the following Provincial 
Associations who have made arrangements to have the CCA Book 
Store at their conferences and meetings: British Columbia, Alberta, 
Manitoba, Ontario, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Newfound¬ 
land. 

A research project of the Publications Committee, funded 
through Fitness Canada, is being carried out by Jack Zoubie. The 
purpose of this research is to investigate the potential market for a 
new publication concerning family camping. 

We are delighted with the increased interest in promoting the 
CCA Book Store across the country and appreciate each member’s 
contribution. We would like to encourage the membership to 
become involved in the Publications Committee by: (a) writing 
reviews of new publications for the CCA magazine and, (b) advising 
us of any title found useful which should be sold through the CCA 
Book Store. 

The Committee would like to thank Irene Knapp* CCA secretary 
who makes our volunteer contribution so much easier and more 
pleasant. 

Wendy Wren and Judy Richards 


PUBLIC RELATIONS AND 
PROMOTION COMMITTEE 

The main thrust of efforts for this committee is the promotion and 
success of National Camping Day - now in its second year. 

As you may remember, last year a workshop was held for provin¬ 
cial representatives in January and these people became the “team” 
who worked on NCD. Last year the time of the chairman was spent 
chiefly in keeping these people enthused, reminded and working. 

For NCD 1984 we chose a different direction. Knowing our team 
was well educated in their roles and able to tackle the public relations 
on a provincial basis, our approach this year was to back this up with 
national coverage. At the January meeting, the CCA Executive 
approved consultation with a PR firm. With their help, we distributed 
a press kit to major newspapers across Canada as well as to 
television stations. Terry Burkhalter from Manitoba prepared a 
radio spot which was sent out with a release and a letter to 70 radio 
stations across Canada. We know that this resulted in interviews in 
Manitoba and Alberta. Jocelyn Palm did interviews out West, and by 
phone to Quebec, and Marjorie Booth appeared on Canada AM - 
due, in part, to a magazine article done earlier in the year with the 
Protect Yourself Magazine. 

Individuals should be singled out who participated in a big way to 
make this year so successful. Thanks to Terry Burkhalter for this 
work on the tapes, and for a poster design which was sent to 1,000 
camping alumni on NCD. Marjorie Booth spent hours working with 
the PR firm in Toronto and helped the chairman, in Montreal, 
coordinate with them and the provincial representatives. As always, 
special appreciation must go to Jocelyn Palm whose initiative and 
drive have caused NCD to be. She also stands in the way of critics 
and helps field all the questions, giving those working assurance and 
support. 

In 1984 it is our intent to have another workshop for new 
provincial representatives, to broaden the team, and the provincial 
experience on public relations. This year our key areas of attack 
were the national media and Ontario. Next year a renewed team 
should be able to make strides on all fronts. 

NCD is hard work. To create a national effort, to highlight our 
activities and to re-educate media and parents about the importance 
of camp choice and early preparation is an almost impossible task. 
Perhaps that is why we continue. As persons who meet challenges 
every day, almost impossible tasks may be what we handle best. 

Mamie Ellis 


STANDARDS TASK FORCE 

The Standards Task Force members have had some information 
sharing over the past year. Communication of revised, updated 
standards or desired practices has been shared as well as process 
information as to how standards are being interpreted or enacted in 
various provinces. 

Requests have come from Mexico, the USA, and South America 
for general information. In addition, recreation-specific requests, eg. 
aquatics, come in on a regular basis. 

Objectives for the fall include a new provincial comparison of 
existing practices, the education of visitors, and an examination of 
the process of accreditation. 

Special thanks to those provinces that have been consistent in 
maintaining communication. 


Brian Law

Do you believe in abortion? 

Card 1 - From a 8 year old to a Counsellor who 
strongly believes in pro-life, and is against abor¬ 
tion, except in extreme medical or emotional 
situations. 

Card 2 - From a 8 year old to a Counsellor who 
believes in the right of the female to obtain an 
abortion when she wishes. 

Card 3 - From a 15 year old to a Counsellor who 
strongly believes in pro-life and is against 
abortion, except in extreme medical or emotional 
situations. 

Card 4 - From a 15 year old to a Counsellor who 
strongly believes in the right of the female to 
obtain an abortion whenever she wishes. 

Topic - Use of Drugs. 

Do you smoke pot? 

Card 1 - From a 10 year old to a Counsellor who 
smokes marijuana or hashish quite regularly. 
Card 2 - From a 10 year old to a Counsellor who 
has tried pot once or twice, but is fairly opposed 
to the practice. 

Card 3 - From a 15 year old to a Counsellor who 
often smokes pot or hashish. 


BOOK REVIEW 

by: Michael Kenny 

“Outdoor Safety & Survival” 

by: Ministry of Lands, Parks and Housing. 
Government of B.C. 

This 153 page, 14 chapter pocket sized book¬ 
let is a “mini Bible” for the outdoor enthusiast, 
one that should be brought along on every trip. 
Even if you don’t require it, it makes excellent 
bed time reading as you sit curled up next to a 
warm campfire dreaming of wild places. 

The chapters of the book give a thorough 
overview of the basic information one requires 
when entering the back country. 

Starting off with a short introduction in the 
psychology of survival, the authors move on to a 
concise eight page chapter on clothing and 
equipment. A short section on travel tips includ¬ 
ing winter travel and how to keep warm is very 
helpful and sensibly points out that if you are 
lost, sometimes the best solution is to stay put. 

The chapters on Finding Your Direction, 
Shelter Building, and Hypothermia have made 
good use of diagrams and charts in addition to 
comprehensive written material. The chapter on 
First Aid covers most of the minor afflictions that 
will occur in back country, but as the authors 
take pains to point out- take a complete first aid 
course before venturing out and when you do 
go, “be prepared” for the worst 

The book uses a common sense perspective 
to outdoor safety- it stresses preparation; how¬ 
ever, if you do find yourself in trouble, take a hold 
of yourself and utilize the resources around you. 
This booklet will be of use to all travellers, 
novice or expert, whatever their mode of travel 
may be. Read It - It might be your life that you 
save. 


Card 4 - From a 15 year old to a Counsellor who 
has had a friend severely mentally impaired by 
the use of non-medical drugs, but is not opposed 
to the experimenting with pot and hashish. 

Topic - Homosexuality. 

Do you think someone who is gay should be 
allowed to be a Minister? 

Card 1 - From all year old to a Counsellor who 
has few problems with homosexual being 
ordained by the Church. 

Card 2 - From a 11 year old to a Counsellor who 
strongly objects to having a known homosexual 
as a Minister of a Church. 

Card 3 - From a 16 year old camper or LIT. to a 
Counsellor who has few problems with a homo¬ 
sexual being ordained by the Church. 

Card 4 - From a 16 year old camper or L.I.T. to a 
Counsellor who strongly objects to having a 
known homosexual as a Minister of a Church. 

Topic - Censorship. 

Do you believe in censorship of movies , books, 
T.V. magazines? 

Card 1 - From a 10 year old to a Counsellor who 
feels that there should be No censorship, but 
also believes there should be controlled access 


to anyone under the legal age. 

Card 2 - From a 10 year old to a Counsellor who 
believes the government has the responsibility 
to censor - and indeed increase censorship. 
Card 3 - From a 15 year old to a Counsellor who 
feels it is an intrusion on the rights of any 
individual to censor anything. 

Card 4 - From a 15 year old to a Counsellor who 
strongly believes lack of censorship increases 
crimes of violence and sexual perversion - 
therefore censorship is a must. 

The above are merely sample topics for 
discussion. In planning this event, the Director 
can write his or her own cards. 

Additional questions might be: 

• Do you believe in Hell? 

• Should someone charged with driving while 
drunk be jailed immediately? 

• Even though Canada is a committed member 
of NATO, should we allow Cruise Missile Test¬ 
ing over our soil? 

• Did you get drunk on your day-off yesterday? 

• Does a person have a right to terminate his/ 
her life? 


CANADIAN 

CONSERVATION 

DIRECTORY 

by: Jean Funk, Environment 
Chairperson 

Ever wonder who else is working to safeguard 
Canada’s environment? The Canadian Nature 
Federation’s non-government organ¬ 
izations concerned with environmental issues. 

Organizations are described in the following 
categories: 

Provincial, natioal, and international 
organizations 

Environmental advisory councils 
Provincial, federal, inter-governmental 
agencies 
Nature centres 
Museums of natural history 
Professional organizations 
Environmental lawyers 
Environmental consulting firms. 

The date established, purpose, number of 
members, serialized and specialized publica¬ 
tions, and recent activities of each organization 
are detailed. 

Your Directory may be purchased for $5.00 
plus 50$ handling charge by writing to: 
Canadian Nature Federation 
75 Albert Street Suite 203, 

Ottawa, Ontario KIP 6G1 

Available from CCA Bookstore: 

$4.95 plus $1.50 shipping 


POEM 



UNITY 

Jesus help us live in peace, 

From our blindness set us free. 
Fill us with your healing love; 

Help us live in unity. 

Many times we disagree, 

O'er what’s right or wrong to do; 
It’s so hard to really see 
From the other’s point of view. 

How we long for power and fame, 
Seeking every earthly thing; 

We forget the one who came 
As a servant not a king.

the National Recreation and Park Association 
the National Society for Internships and Experiential Education 
the World Alliance of YMCAs 
the World Association of Girl Guides and Girl Scouts 


Purpose 

The Second International Camping Congress is an event to bring together the 
practitioners of the outdoor experience movement from many nations and 
related organizations to examine the elements of our fragile world which 
challenge the organized camping, environmental, and experiential education 
community to impact participants for future action. 


Specifically, the Congress shall seek: 


To share current knowledge and techniques in organized camping and outdoor 
environmental and experiential education. 

To consider global issues such as peace and conservation which can be impacted 
by the outdoor experience movement. 

To explore with a global perspective the future trends of the camping, out¬ 
door environmental and experiential education movement and the implication 
on culture. 

To foster an atmosphere of personal sharing across international and inter¬ 
disciplinary lines. 

If you are a member of one of the aforementioned organizations, watch for 
further information from your organization. If you are not already a member 
of one of these organizations and wish to be placed on the mailing list for the 
Congress, write Second International Camping Congress, c/o American Camp¬ 
ing Association, Bradford Woods, Martinsville, IN 46151. 



Memorable Quotes from "Blackie" Blackstock 



by: Adele and Harry Ebbs 

C.R. BLACKSTOCK, 'Blackie' B.Sc. (McGill) 
L.L.D. (York) 

Blackie was at Pickering College in 1928, 
during the same period as the late Taylor 
Statten, who realized the contribution he would 
make on staff at Camp Ahmek. However, this 
had to wait because Blackie was a Kitchikewana 
‘original’. He started the first year of that V camp 
on Beausoleil Island in 1921 as a very young 
counsellor, when Ernie Thurlow, boys work 
secretary for Simcoe County, was the director. 
Blackie rose to assistant director when Win 
Smith took over. He gave input to the current 
research being done by the Society of Camp 
Directors, of which he was a Founding Fellow, 
when he alleged that canoe trippers should be 
trained to handle risk and to anticipate it. For his 
contribution to the Ontario Camping Association 
he earned an Honourary Life Membership. 

Hedid some summercoursesatWisconsin in 
out-door education, and finished his formal 
education at McGill, earning a Bachelor of 
Science. His Honour Doctorate was granted at 
York University in 1974. 

In 1936 he directed Bolton Camp and for some 
years after that was the inspired and creative 
director of Camp Pinecrest. His interest and 
education in the out-of-doors he applied at 
Pickering College by exposing the boys to the 
first winter school-camping for a number of 
seasons at Limberlost Lodge. 

For a man of his interests it was natural to 
seek fulfillment, along with compatible partners, 
by establishing a camp of their own. Since the 
beginning, in 1940, Camp Mazinaw has ex¬ 
pressed Blackie’s basic philosophy of excel¬ 
lence in endeavour and encouragement to all 
individuals whatever their ability. With the chal¬ 
lenge of the great Bon Echo rock always in view, 
he has soared above to reach for the stars - and 
led all who would follow. 

His influence has been felt all across Canada, 
first through the Canadian Red Cross and 
latterly for many years as executive secretary of 
the Canadian Association of Physical and Health 
Education. Even in retirement he was appointed 
consultant to the Sports Centre in Ottawa. 


The following quotes are excerpts from the 
Camping Archives at Trent University: 

Camping’s Adventure 

“There wasn’t any real idea of going out and 
competing against nature for survival or some¬ 
thing! This wasn’t the idea behind most of the 
people, was it? I think it was more for enjoyment 
and well, maybe, an escape from the city.” 

“The adventure that any of us, no matter what 
age, but anybody that is young in mind or spirit 
will seek these. Like climb Everest. Why? You 
can’t answer that question. You accept a chal¬ 
lenge from nature, not to master it, but to live with 
it” 

“The real thing about it is that we are children of 
the world and we live with the other creatures 
that are in it. And sure there’s a survival element 
to it. You’ve got to be able to read the wind if 
you're going to canoe on some lakes, you’ve got 
to be able to read the water if you’re going to 
travel some streams or rivers; you’ve got to be 
able to read the sky, or stars... if you’re going to 
find your way around in the bush; and it just 
depends on where your curiosity leads you.” 

Importance of Rules 

“Those of us who have been teachers, and 
especially teachers of physical education - 
we’ve noticed this change, this disregard for 
rules. Rules are there to make any kind of 
competition human. You can go out and play 
football, and if you’re playing for money, the 
chances are you’ll do a lot of things that you 
wouldn’t if you were out in the corner lot 
throwing a ball around. Now in the one case, 
you have a set of officials that endeavours to 
rule everybody that’s playing, and their actions. 
But in the other case on the corner lot, or on the 
lawn, you rule yourselves. You know ruddy well 
that you’re not going to do something to the 
other guy that he might do back to you, but 
better. Now this kind of rule was a ruling we’ve 
been brought up to respect. And even as a kid 
my parents would not let me get vicious with 
animals, whether they were domesticated, or 
wild. And so I wouldn’t think of pushing a horse 
beyond what I should know is its capability. 
Cause I’ve been brought up to recognize. Or I 
couldn’t go shooting, and just kill for the sake of 
killing. So I’m not a hunter. But I can live with 
those animals when I get out in the bush. So 
conservation isn’t something that needs to be 
taught; you expose people to the situation, and 
they’re sharp enough to see ... well gee, some¬ 
body’s mucking up the water! Or look at all those 
trees; somebody left a fire, and they’re all burned 
down. That hurts. Or you go along and see a 
bunch of fish up on the shore beside a fire¬ 
place, and they’re left there to rot. Why not leave 
them in the water? You’re not going to use it. You 
know, man is ... it still comes from heaven, and 
you can only take what you can use and the rest 
of it will go bad.” 

A Tough and Chellenging Interviewee 

Q: Do you have trouble getting qualified staff 
members to work at your camp? 

B.B.: “What do you mean by qualified?" 


Q: Well first of all, they must have a mature, 
responsible attitude... 

B.B.: “How do you measure that?” 

Q: The way they will carry out their actions - if 
you ask them to do something, you know that it 
will be done. And it will be done well. And if they 
can’t do it, they will try. 

B.B.: “Are you a qualified person?” 

Q: I believe so, yes. 

B.B.: “In whose opinion?” 

Q: In my own! After all these years of... 

B.B.: “If I was a camp director and hiring you for 
the summer, which I well might do, how would I 
know that you were, before I saw you in action, 
at Mazinaw?” 

Q: That’s very difficult to tell. You could go by the 
sales-pitch that I could give you, and my back¬ 
ground. 

B.B.: “I might go by that.” 

Q: By sales-pitch, some people can come on 
very sincere, and when they get into the real 
situation they may have been sincere originally, 
but when they get into the real situation they 
might find it too much to cope with. This is what I 
mean by a sales-pitch. 

B.B.: “Well, I don’t pay very much attention to 
sales-pitches." 

Q: Well, what do you look for in a person when 
you hire them? 

B.B.: “A person that’s interested in other people, 
more than himself.” 

His Philosophy 

“Well, I don’t care where the campsite is, as long 
as it provides an opportunity for people to learn 
to live in it. You could have a camp in the city, if 
your purpose was to have a kid learn to live in 
the city, comfortably, with others, eh? So really 
the site doesn’t matter. It’s what you take in the 
way of staff to the site. And they must have 
enough imagination, and initiative to exploit, if 
you like, but to develop that particular site to 
achieve the purpose which you set for your¬ 
selves. You can choose any purpose you like. 
Blair Fraser and Sigurd Olson, and Eric Morse- 
have camped all over the ancient riverways of 
this country. They know it. And they lived there. 
And they found out how others lived there, and 
travelled through it. Lome Brown has a camp up 
on the High Savannahs of - in the caribou 
country in British Columbia. It’s a small camp 
like this. Purposes aren’t quite the same, speci¬ 
fically; but fundamentally they are. So, I just don’t 
think that we, as people, and particularly Cana¬ 
dians, should not enjoy living in any part of it; 
and exploring it, for the fun of that exploration, 
and to satisfy our curiosity. The most important 
part is that people should know: The kingdom is 
where 2 or 3 are gathered together in My name’. 
In wonderment and in awe at the loveliness of 
life. And what other purpose is there for being 
alive? If you don’t know your world, you’ll be 
perfectly safe, if you just stay in one spot. The 
most important quality that a leader has is his 
curiosity. He doesn’t centre on himself; he 
centres on other things. All will come back to 
him as he gives." 


13 



KIDNEY KIDS 
CAMP OUT 
OVERNIGHT 

by: Dave Sands 
lllahee Northwoods Camp 

Camping programs have recently added a 
new dimension to the lives of children with 
severe kidney failure. Now, thanks to meticulous 
planning by lllahee Northwoods Camp staff, 
these boys and girls can even take overnight 
canoe trips. 

For the past three years lllahee Northwoods 
Camp has provided a two-week camping experi¬ 
ence for about 40 children with severe kidney 
disorders. The children come from across 
Canada and are sponsored by the Kidney Foun¬ 
dation of Canada, lllahee is a camp for children 
whose activity is limited by their health and it 
annually provides a camping experience for 
about 200 children with a variety of medical 
conditions. 

Life at camp for the child with a kidney 
condition is circumscribed by the demands of 
treatment, either haemo-dialysis or continuous 
ambulatory peritineal dialysis, which takes a 
great lump of time out of their day. But with the 
dialysis unit right on the camp grounds treatment 
time is kept to a minimum. The unit is staffed for 
that one period by renal specialists (doctor, 
nurses and technicians) provided by the Kidney 
Foundation which also raised the money to con¬ 
struct and equip the building. 

In November 1982, we got our senior camp 
staff together to brainstorm ways to make their 
stay more meaningful for these campers. It was 
decided to organize an overnight camping trip¬ 
an unlikely activity for a child accustomed to 
spending much of his life in hospitals. They 
would fit the trips between periods of dialysis or 
medication taking off after morning treatment 
one day, returning for treatment the next day. 


Planning the Trip 

Every detail was thought through carefully in 
advance. A complete medical kit was assembled 
and extra medical staff assigned to the trip. With 
advance menu planning and pre-packaging the 
food was suited to their dietic needs, but still 
provided an outdoor and tripping flavour... stew, 
french toast, puddings, etc. Contingency arrange¬ 
ments were made for possible emergencies. 
Once all plans were complete Sands proceeded 
to sell the idea of the trip to the skeptical renal 
medical staff, who finally gave permission for 
the first trip. 

As a result, a group of twelve campers, five 
with kidney disorders, set ouf from lllahee in a 
pioneer camping venture. They were accom¬ 
panied by three camping staff, a renal nurse and 
a regular camp nurse. Travelling in war or 
freighter canoes, they were shadowed by a 
distant motor boat ... just in case. One staff 
person, the tripper, knew that there was a truck 
parked near the remote campsite and a phone 
was also available, but these were not needed. 


Camping Out 

The trip was like any other camping trip at 
lllahee. The campers learned to build fires and 
cook their food. In the evening they had a 
singsong around the campfire and then slept on 
the ground in tents they had learned to pitch 
themselves. After preparing and enjoying a 
healthy morning breakfast they set out again in 
their canoes, heading back to camp and their 
very necessary medication and treatment. 

For the children it was a complete new world, 
one they never had thought of entering. They 
were able to go home and tell their friends and 
they, too, had been camping outdoors... at night 
... in the wild. For the renal medical staff it was an 
eye-opener. Medically, the children had not 
suffered, but their self-confidence had soared. 
They saw themselves accomplishing normal, 
even a little risky, tasks and camp took on a new 
meaning to them. The medical team became 
staunch supporters of the trips and two more 
were undertaken before the boys and girls left 
camp. The out-trips will now be an integral part 
of the program for children with renal conditions. 


Rabies - A Problem for Children s Camps 


By: J.H. Ebbs, M.D. 

The majority of children's camps are in areas 
away from cities and towns - in the country, 
rural areas and often close to or in wilderness 
districts. 

Wild animals are numerous but only a per¬ 
centage are seen. 

Rabies was known for a long time in the Arctic 
and northern regions of Canada. I the 1950’s, it 
spread south and east across the country, 
affecting mostly dogs and recently cows. 

Prior to 1950 there were a few cases of rabies 
reported each year. The peak occurred between 
1953 and 1958, while now there are about 1,000 
per year. 

In addition to cattle and dogs, it also occurs in 
cats, horses, sheep, goats and bats (the majority 


in western Canada and Ontario). The majority of 
rabid skunks were reported in Ontario and 
Saskatchewan (32%) while foxes (62%) were in 
Ontario. 

Rabies in wild animals rises in the autumn as 
the young males spread out, while in early 
spring the females are affected during and 
following the litter. 

While rabies is now largely controlled in cats 
and dogs by a higher percent of immunizations, 
it is still necessary to treat several hundred 
people a year who have been bitten or exposed 
to rabid animals. Fortunately the new vaccines 
and serums do not cause the severe illness 
which was common in the past. 

At camp, all persons, bitten, scratched or in 


contact with a suspected animal, should as 
soon as possible have wounds, scratches and 
skin washed with soap and water or detergent 
and given a tetanus injection as well as antibio¬ 
tics and an application of alcohol or iodine to the 
wound. 

Prevention of rabies risk is to get rid of stray 
and suspicious animals - report them and if 
killed preserve the head intact for examination. 

The seriousness of the disease demands 
strict practices for all personnel in camp with 
regard to animals. 

1. Don’t have domestic animals in camp which 
have not been vaccinated. 

2. Avoid having pets in camp. 

3. Caution all campers and staff to avoid contact 
with all animals - especially young ones.

YOUTH CAMP 

DIRECTOR 

INSTITUTE 

by: Ceciley Parker, 

Institute Committee 

1985 is the International Youth Year. To cel¬ 
ebrate the occasion the Canadian Camping 
Association has organized a Youth Camp Direc¬ 
tor’s Institute, to be held January 31st to Febru¬ 
ary 3rd. 1985, at Bolton Camp and Conference 
Centre, Ontario. 

Focusing on Youth, the four day event will 
address a variety of subjects under the theme 
headings of: 

Youth - in a changing society 

Youth - as world citizens 

Youth - their development as leaders 

Youth’s - values of today, directions for 
tomorrow. 

Some specific topics to be discussed include: 

• youth as a minority 

• volunteerism 

• stress 

• changing family structure 

• addiction 

• women’s emergence 

• communication (human and computer) 

• camping as a lifetime activity 

• impact of media on developing values 

• developing responsibility, empathy, 
sympathy. 

Leadership 

The organizing committee is currently en¬ 
deavouring to draw together internationally 
renowned speakers. Delegates from across 
Canada, representing new and experienced 
Directors, will be able to share experiences and 
ideas through workshops and discussions. 

Cost 

The $145.00 registration fee is all inclusive. It 
covers the Institute fee, accommodation, meals 
(Thursday dinner through to Sunday lunch), and 
return transportation from Pearson International 
Airport to Bolton Camp and Conference Centre. 
While delegates will be responsible for return 
transportation from their home province, there 
are some airfare subsidies available. 

Further information will be available soon 
through your Provincial Camping Association. 
Since there will be a limit on the number of 
places available, we urge you to mark your 
calendar and apply early so that you may be part 
of this national gathering of directors. Institute 
registration information will be available by 
September 1984.

CAMPING ...THE LAST WORD! 

by Kirsty Griffiths, Camping Coordinator, Ontario March of Dimes 


First of all let me commend the CCA for devoting 
almostan entire issue to camping opportunities 
for disabled people. The issue of integration vs. 
segregation continues to be a difficult one for 
many people to come to terms with, including 
camp directors. 

Sylvia Haynes’ article “Camping is Fun! And it 
is for Everyone!” assists camp directors by 
identifying many factors they should consider. 
The intent of the article is excellent in: 1) promot¬ 
ing a camping experience for disabled young¬ 
sters in an integrated setting; 2) encouraging 
directors to plan and prepare beforehand; 3) 
encouraging the design of accessible facilities 
with a view to the future. 

Being involved myself in a camping program 
for physically disabled adults I read the article 
with interest. Often those of us working with 
disabled people get caught up in the language 
and jargon of the discipline. It is my opinion that 
once the attitudinal barrier has been passed the 
process of integration, although involving much 
effort, is really not that difficult in a camping 
situation. It is for this reason that I feel I must 
comment, expand and attempt to clarify for the 
uninitiated the points raised in this article. 

The author asks “What % of disabled/non- 
disabled?" It occurs to me that rather than 
setting a %, each Camp Director needs to deter¬ 
mine what number of disabled children can be 
provided with a good experience at his/her 
camp - taking into consideration the child's dis¬ 
ability, the view of parents of non-disabled 
children attending camp, number of staff, the 
physical site and the type of program the camp 
offers. Consideration must also be given to the 
physical, social and emotional needs of the 
potential camper. 

The author asks “... a pool - is it warm enough 
to stand in for at least 40 minutes? - suggest 86”. 
A heated pool is of course ideal but this shouldn't 
discourage the child from swimming, nor the 
Camp Director from accepting thechildatcamp. 
The disabled child has as much right to get cold 
and then feel the warmth of a fire and hot 
chocolate as any other child! However, common 
sense and flexibility should prevail. In a child 
with Cerebral Palsy for example - the muscles 
will tighten in cold water and this could be 
painful if the child gets very chilled. 

The author asks “Are bunk beds OK? Yes... 
as long as they are accessible from both sides”. 
Yes, bunk beds are feasible, but you may not 
have access from both sides. Again don’t let this 
deter you! Some children using wheelchairs 
transfer better from one side or the other. Let him 
pick thei r bed on either the right or the left side of 
the room or switch the pillow end when the 
make up their bed to accommodate their “good" 
side. A side rail might be appropriate in some 
cases. If this is not possible and the child is used 
to this security - just “bank” the mattress 
towards the wall. (i.e. put pillows or rolled up 
blankets between the mattress and the frame 


along the outside edge so the mattress is gently 
sloped to the wall. Lifting someone in and out of 
a bunk bed is inconvenient but it can be done if 
you are committed to having that child at camp. 

There are many resources available to assist 
a camp director with the proper dimensions for 
the physical plant. I have attempted to list some 
of these at the end of my letter. Removable 
ramps may be necessary for some camps but 
the ideal is to build them well and have them 
permanent. Ramps can be used by everyone 
but stairs present a barrier to some. 

The author describes the slope of the ramp as 
“One foot rise in 12 inches". I take issue with this 
description. It should read 1 inch rise in 12 
inches or more clearly stated for every inch rise 
the ramp should extend 12 inches out. For 
example, if the step into a building is 6 inches 
high you will need a 6 foot ramp. If a long ramp is 
needed there can be an L shape with a landing. 
There should be a double railing on both sides 
of the ramp and a “lip” running along the edges 
of the ramp on the floor is advisable. A wheel¬ 
chair must not be able to fall off a ramp or go 
through a railing. 

The points regarding level of basins, soap 
dishes and mirrors in washrooms are well 
taken. However no mention is made of toilet 
stalls. Wider doors that open out as well as 
enlarged cubicles are needed. Again refer to the 
resources that are available for dimensions. 

The author states that “Picnic tables... can be 
accessible”. For the uninitiated, the how is 
answered by simply removing the bench seat 
from one side to allow someone in a wheelchair 
to reach the table. 

The author asks "How much of the rails 
should be changed?" I assume the author is 
referring to hand rails? There should be hand 
rails on both sides of stairways and they should 
be round, like piping rather than a 2 x 4 which is 
often used. 

The author’s point is well taken in suggesting 
you have a disabled person assist you in recom¬ 
mending adjustments to your site. But remember 
what may be right for one disabled individual 
may be a hindrance to another. Again it is advis¬ 
able to follow universally accepted standards 
and adjust to suit your own situation. 

The question about staff is raised. I fully agree 
that staff be prepared and I believe it is impera¬ 
tive that all the staff in your camp receive some 
basic practical and attitudinal training, not just 
those assigned to work with the disabled 
campers. Depending on the size of your staff 
and the scope of your program of integration 
this could be done in a morning or over a couple 
of days. The most important thing to remember 
is that your staff do not need to be specifically 
hired for their previous experience with disabled 
children. By contacting your local associations 
who work with sight or hearing impaired chil¬ 
dren, developmental^ handicapped people or 
those individuals with physical disabilities you 


should find a wealth of information and people 
more than likely willing to come to your staff 
orientation period and provide this training. 

With regards to “parents’ apprehensions of 
mainstreaming”. Assuming these are parents of 
your non-disabled children this is indeed a 
major consideration. This issue is far too large 
to discuss here but some things you might con¬ 
sider when integrating for the first time are: 1) a 
letter to the parents of your non-disabled 
campers outlining your intentions by discussing 
the positive nature of the program and assuring 
them their child is going to receive the same 
care and attention that he/she always does; 2) 
hold a meeting for parents - have an outside 
resource person available - perhaps another 
camp director who has been through the pro¬ 
cess or someone from a local association 
working with disabled persons. You certainly 
don’t want to lose your regular clientele but I 
believe with the proper approach and a carefully 
thought out program you should receive a 
generally positive response. 

For the most part the author has used the 
words disabled and handicapped as adjectives. 
However at times in the article - perhaps, for 
abbreviation sake, they are used as nouns. For 
example “Do not use labels on handicapped - 
this arouses immediate fears”. Although a subtle 
distinction (and probably very unintentional) 
when referring to people with disabilities we all 
must make a very conscious effort to use these 
words as an adjective, always using words like 
children, people or individual as the noun. The 
words handicapped and disabled seem to be 
used interchangeably in the article. Our experi¬ 
ence has shown that the word handicapped is 
not generally accepted by those people with 
physical disabilities. Your readers might be 
interested in knowing that the derivation of the 
word comes from cap in hand - a person 
begging for money. A child with a physical dis¬ 
ability is just that - a child or person first and 
foremost. It should be the person that stands out 
to you - not the disability. 

One area not discussed which I feel is ex¬ 
tremely important is the preparation of the dis¬ 
abled youngster. A meeting with the child and 
his/her parents and the camp director is impor¬ 
tant. The family needs to find out about the 
camp, your philosophy of the program, staffing 
and decide if your camp will meet the needs of 
their child. The camp director must find out 
about the physical needs of the child as well as 
the child’s expectations, fears, interests, etc. 
Sounds like something you would do with any 
child considering your camp! The last thing you 
want is to find that you can’t meet the needs of 
the disabled child after he/she arrives at your 
camp. I have found that a curious mind which 
continually asks questions is very helpful. 

For camp directors attempting to integrate for 
the first time - the more detailed and clear 
See Camping: The Last Word - page 2
